storyline: A star's color is a thermometer you can read with your own eyes. Everything that glows, from a stove ring to the Sun, sends out a broad spread of colors, and the hotter it gets the more that spread tips from red toward blue. So the stops climb the scale in order: an ember-red star at the cool end, then orange, then the Sun's own yellow, then white. Blue-white comes last, at the hot end, where the eye's thermometer starts to run out of range, and when the sky allows, a pair closes the night with two temperatures in a single view. At every stop you judge the color first, against the one before it, and only then learn what it means in kelvins and why. By the end you are not being told the temperatures of the stars; you are reading them.

STAR-MuCep.question: Why does the Garnet Star look redder than almost any other star you can see?
STAR-MuCep.why: Every thermometer needs a bottom mark, and the Garnet Star supplies one with a red so deep that every later star will look hotter beside it.
STAR-MuCep.look: Find it a little south of the halfway point between Alderamin and ζ Cephei, in Cepheus. Among the white stars around it, it glows a deep orange-red, and nudging the focus slightly soft spreads it into a small disk where the color is easier to judge.
STAR-MuCep.answer: Its surface runs at under two-thirds of the Sun's temperature, and a glow that cool sends out far more red than blue; dust along the way reddens it a little more. Any star that looks less red than this one, you can now say, is hotter.
STAR-MuCep.story: William Herschel named it for its color in the 1780s, and part of that color is borrowed. On its way to us its light crosses dust, which scatters blue more readily than red, the same physics that reddens a sunset. Astronomers measure how much by comparing the color they see with the temperature the star's spectrum gives. The gap shows it would look a shade less red without the dust, though still far redder than anything around it.

STAR-Betelgeuse.question: What does the orange-red of Betelgeuse say about the temperature of its surface?
STAR-Betelgeuse.why: A good scale starts from a reading you can trust, and Betelgeuse, whose temperature has been measured with unusual care, glows at the cool end where the night begins.
STAR-Betelgeuse.look: Betelgeuse is Orion's eastern shoulder, opposite blue-white Rigel. Turn the focus a little past sharp and the point blooms into a small disk whose orange-red becomes obvious, then swing to Rigel and back to feel how different two temperatures can look.
STAR-Betelgeuse.answer: The color says cool, some 2,200 degrees below the Sun's surface, and the reading has held steady. During the Great Dimming of 2020 its temperature barely changed, so the fade was dust, not cooling, and the color stayed a faithful thermometer.
STAR-Betelgeuse.story: In 1920 Albert Michelson and Francis Pease made Betelgeuse the first star after the Sun to have its width measured, using mirrors spread along a beam across the Mount Wilson telescope. A measured width and the star's total light together say how much each square meter of its surface gives out, and that fixes the temperature with no help from the color. So Betelgeuse became one of the stars against which the color thermometer itself is checked.

STAR-Antares.question: How cool must Antares be to glow this shade of orange-red?
STAR-Antares.why: The thermometer starts with the reddest bright star in Scorpius, a supergiant whose hot blue-white siblings lie scattered around it, ready to fill in the rest of the scale.
STAR-Antares.look: Antares is the red heart of Scorpius. Put it near the edge of the field and defocus slightly: its orange deepens toward red, while the soft gray ball of M4, about two and a half Moon-widths to the west, looks colorless by comparison.
STAR-Antares.answer: Antares needs less than two-thirds of the Sun's surface temperature to glow like this, because a surface that cool sends out far more red than blue. That it still shines so brightly means it must be huge, about 680 times the Sun's width, but the color itself reports only the heat.
STAR-Antares.story: Antares is near enough and large enough that its disk can be measured directly. In 2013 astronomers linked the telescopes of the Very Large Telescope to measure its width in the sky. They added up all the light it sends us, and from the two worked out how much each square meter of its surface must give out. That fixes the temperature without trusting the color at all, and the answer lands where the orange-red says it should.

HR8775.question: Why is one corner of the Great Square orange-red while the others are white?
HR8775.why: The Great Square is a ready-made color chart, and Scheat, its one warm corner, gives the scale its cool end.
HR8775.look: Scheat is the north-west corner of the Great Square of Pegasus. In binoculars it is clearly orange-red; swing to Markab, the corner directly south, and back, and the difference in tint jumps out.
HR8775.answer: Scheat's surface is only about 3,700 K, and a glow that cool is dominated by red light, while Markab and Alpheratz burn at more than 10,000 K. You are seeing a gap of thousands of degrees as a simple change of color.
HR8775.story: Astronomers turn that impression into a number, the color index, by measuring a star's brightness through a blue filter and again through a yellow one and taking the difference. For Scheat the blue reading comes out well over a magnitude fainter than the yellow, while for Markab the two nearly agree, and tables built from stars of known temperature convert each difference into kelvins.

HR8636.question: How much cooler is the Crane's red star than its blue-white neighbor?
HR8636.why: In Grus the whole thermometer fits in two quick glances, and the reading starts here, with the Crane's ember-colored star.
HR8636.look: Put Tiaki and Alnair in turn at the center of your binoculars. Tiaki is a deep orange-red, Alnair a clean blue-white, and a slight defocus makes both colors richer.
HR8636.answer: Alnair runs at about 13,200 K, nearly four times Tiaki's temperature, and your eye turns that difference into the contrast between ember and ice.
HR8636.story: Every glowing body has a color at which its light peaks, and the peak slides toward shorter waves as the temperature climbs. Tiaki's peak lies in the infrared, beyond the reach of the eye, so the visible part of its glow is the rising red slope; Alnair's peak lies in the ultraviolet, so you see the falling blue slope of its glow instead. Ember and ice are the two sides of the same curve.

HR4763.question: Why is the top of the Southern Cross orange while its other stars are blue-white?
HR4763.why: The Southern Cross holds one warm color among its blue-white stars, and that warm star is where the scale begins.
HR4763.look: Center the top star of the Cross and compare its warm orange-red with blue-white Acrux at the foot. Defocus slightly and the color jumps out; the faint white star just north-east is a background star, not a partner.
HR4763.answer: Gacrux's surface is only about 3,700 K, under two-thirds of the Sun's, so its glow leans red; Acrux and Mimosa run above 20,000 K, which is why one small cross spans nearly the whole scale. The color told you which star was the odd one out before any spectrum did.
HR4763.story: The temperature of a red giant like Gacrux can be measured almost directly. Linked telescopes, which see detail far finer than any single one, measure the width of its tiny disk. Adding up all the light it sends us across every color then says how much each square meter of that disk gives out, which only one temperature can produce. That reading agrees with the color, which is why astronomers trust color for the countless stars too small to measure.

HR337.question: How cool is the ruddy star in the middle of Andromeda's chain?
HR337.why: Andromeda's chain of stars runs from ruddy to golden to blue-white, and the reading begins at its ruddy middle.
HR337.look: Mirach is the middle bright star of Andromeda's chain, a ruddy orange point in binoculars. Sweep along the chain to Alpheratz and back and the difference in warmth is plain.
HR337.answer: Mirach's surface is about 3,800 K, cooler than the Sun by some 2,000 degrees, which tips its light toward red. Almach, at the end of the chain, looks golden rather than ruddy, the sign of a surface a few hundred degrees hotter.
HR337.story: Mirach's spectrum is crossed by faint bands of titanium oxide, a molecule that falls apart in any hotter atmosphere, so finding it is a temperature reading of its own. The letters astronomers use to rank stars, running O, B, A, F, G, K, M from hot to cool, were sorted out largely from clues like this, and Mirach sits at the start of the last and coolest class.

HR6056.question: Why does Yed Prior look redder than its partner, Yed Posterior?
HR6056.why: Two stars sharing one binocular field make the gentlest possible start to a color lesson, and the redder of the pair opens the scale.
HR6056.look: Yed Prior and Yed Posterior sit about one and a half degrees apart in Ophiuchus, an easy pair in one field. δ is distinctly orange-red and ε yellower, and a slight defocus sharpens the contrast.
HR6056.answer: Yed Prior's surface is only about 3,800 K, so its light leans red, while its yellower partner is a warmer giant. Their distances differ, but distance dims a star without changing its tint, so the colors still read as two honest temperatures.
HR6056.story: A star's tint survives any distance, but dust is another matter: fine grains scatter blue light more than red, as the air does at sunset, so a star seen through a lot of dust looks redder than it really is. Yed Prior and its partner are near enough that little dust lies in front of either, so the contrast between them belongs to the stars and not to the space in between.

HR1607.question: How can a star be red enough to be called crimson?
HR1607.why: To calibrate a thermometer you want its coolest mark, and few stars run cooler than this carbon star, which shows its crimson for only part of its long cycle.
HR1607.look: Drop south from Rigel into Lepus and look about 3½° west-north-west of μ Leporis. Near its maximum it glows a startling deep red among white stars, best judged with short glances; near its minimum it fades beyond binoculars, so treat it as a bonus when it shows.
HR1607.answer: Hind's Crimson Star runs at less than half the Sun's surface temperature, and in air that cool carbon forms molecules and soot that soak up blue light, so its glow is filtered as well as cool. Every star you meet after it will look whiter, because every one of them is hotter.
HR1607.story: When John Russell Hind came upon it in 1845 he compared it to a drop of blood on a black field. A surface this cool sends most of its energy out as infrared, which no eye can see, so the light that reaches you is only the short red tail of a glow that mostly happens out of sight. The color also changes with the star's long cycle and is deepest near its dim point, when the surface is at its coolest.

HR1648.question: Why does W Orionis glow redder than Betelgeuse, its bright neighbor in Orion?
HR1648.why: Orion's thermometer can start even lower than Betelgeuse, with a faint carbon star whose red only binoculars reveal.
HR1648.look: Look about 7° south-west of Bellatrix, Orion's western shoulder. Among the white field stars it stands out as a warm orange-red point, and a slight defocus boosts the color.
HR1648.answer: W Orionis is nearly a thousand degrees cooler than Betelgeuse and smoky with carbon besides, so its light has lost almost all its blue before it leaves the star. It sets a low mark that every other star tonight will beat.
HR1648.story: In most stars there is more oxygen than carbon, and the two lock together into carbon monoxide, leaving no spare carbon to color the light. In W Orionis repeated dredging from the helium-burning depths has tipped that count the other way, and the leftover carbon builds molecules and grains that act like a sooty filter. Temperature sets the starting color, and the soot finishes the job.

HR3541.question: How cool is the red star hiding near the Beehive?
HR3541.why: Near the Beehive hides a star you would pass over if not for its color, and that color makes it the bottom mark of the scale.
HR3541.look: From the Beehive, the misty patch in Cancer between Regulus and the Gemini twins, move about four and a half degrees south-east. X Cancri stands out by its warm red-orange, which seems to deepen the longer you look.
HR3541.answer: X Cancri runs at less than half the Sun's surface temperature, about as cool as any star binoculars can show. Regulus, about 18° to the south-east, runs more than four times hotter, which is nearly the whole span of the scale in two stars.
HR3541.story: Faint red stars play a trick on the eye: the longer you stare, the brighter and redder they seem, because the eye's response to dim red light keeps building while it watches. Variable-star observers learned long ago to judge such stars with quick glances, and X Cancri, with its deep tint, is a good place to catch the effect at work. The color itself is the honest part, the reading of a surface far too cool to glow white.

HR2405.question: Why does one faint star in Auriga glow orange-red among white neighbors?
HR2405.why: Auriga's brilliant stars make a fine scale, but its cool end is a faint carbon star that shows its warmth only in binoculars.
HR2405.look: Look in eastern Auriga, between Capella and the Gemini twins: among white stars, one glows orange-red. Judge its color with short glances rather than a stare, since faint red stars play tricks on a tired eye.
HR2405.answer: UU Aurigae runs at less than half the Sun's surface temperature, so it starts out red, and its carbon-laden air deepens the red further. Capella, a sweep to the west, is nearly twice as hot and glows yellow.
HR2405.story: In the 1860s Angelo Secchi, sorting stars by the patterns in their spectra, set aside a small group whose light was cut by broad dark bands, and those bands turned out to be carbon molecules. Molecules like these hold together only in a cool atmosphere, so the bands are a second thermometer, and in UU Aurigae they agree with the color that this is among the coolest surfaces a binocular star can show.

HR9004.question: Why is TX Piscium so much redder than an ordinary red giant?
HR9004.why: Some red stars owe part of their color to their own smoky air, and TX Piscium, near the Great Square, opens the scale with a reddened glow.
HR9004.look: Find the Circlet, the faint ring of stars south of the Great Square of Pegasus; TX Piscium is the ruddy star just east of it, obvious at once among white field stars. Look away and back, because red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare.
HR9004.answer: TX Piscium is cool enough to glow red on its own, at a little over half the Sun's temperature, and spare carbon in its atmosphere forms soot that soaks up blue and violet as well. Temperature sets the starting color, and the soot pushes it further toward crimson.
HR9004.story: TX Piscium is bright enough to show its color easily, which makes it a good test of how much of a star's tint belongs to its surface and how much to the filter of its own air. Spectra separate the two: the overall shape of the glow gives the temperature, while the dark bands of carbon molecules cut into it show how much light the soot has stolen. Both are needed to explain how red it looks.

STAR-LaSuperba.question: Why did an astronomer name this faint red star the superb one?
STAR-LaSuperba.why: The scale opens with one of the reddest stars in the sky, a color strong enough to show in binoculars though the eye alone barely notices the star.
STAR-LaSuperba.look: From Cor Caroli, below the Big Dipper's handle, head about a third of the way toward Megrez. La Superba is obvious in binoculars as a glowing red-orange ember, and it seems to redden further the longer you hold it.
STAR-LaSuperba.answer: La Superba runs at less than half the Sun's surface temperature, with carbon soot blocking most of the blue that is left, so Angelo Secchi, sorting stars by their spectra, saw an extraordinary red and named it for that. Cor Caroli, blue-white nearby, runs more than four times hotter.
STAR-LaSuperba.story: Ordinary color charts make a carbon star look cooler than it is, because the soot in its air removes blue light that the surface really does send out. Astronomers get around this by measuring the star's tiny disk with linked telescopes and adding up all its light, which yields the temperature without trusting the color. For La Superba the two routes differ, and the difference measures what the carbon has taken.

STAR-Aldebaran.question: How much cooler than the Sun is the orange eye of Taurus?
STAR-Aldebaran.why: The first step up from the deep reds is orange, and Aldebaran shows it against the pale cluster stars of the Hyades, which make its tint easy to judge.
STAR-Aldebaran.look: Aldebaran is the orange eye of Taurus at one tip of the V of the Hyades. Frame the whole V: its warm orange stands apart from the white and pale-yellow cluster stars, and a slight defocus makes the difference plain.
STAR-Aldebaran.answer: Its surface is about 3,900 K, roughly 1,900 degrees cooler than the Sun's, which tips its glow toward orange. θ² Tauri, white in the same field, runs nearly twice as hot.
STAR-Aldebaran.story: Long before anyone could measure a star's temperature, astronomers sorted spectra by their patterns of dark lines, and the order they settled on turned out to be a temperature scale. Cecilia Payne showed why in 1925: nearly every star is made of much the same elements, and what changes from class to class is how hot the gas is, which decides which atoms can absorb which colors. Aldebaran sits well down that scale, where the lines of metals crowd its light.

HR1577.question: Why does one corner of the Auriga pentagon glow orange?
HR1577.why: Auriga's pentagon holds several marks of the scale at once, and its orange corner is the warm one to start from.
HR1577.look: Look at the pentagon of Auriga, with Capella at its top: its south-western corner is ι Aurigae, distinctly orange beside yellowish Capella and white Menkalinan. Defocus slightly and the three colors line up like marks on a scale.
HR1577.answer: ι Aurigae's surface runs roughly 800 degrees cooler than Capella's, and that modest gap is enough to turn yellow into orange. Menkalinan, at about 9,000 K, is the next mark up after Capella.
HR1577.story: A century ago at Harvard, Annie Jump Cannon sorted hundreds of thousands of stars by the dark lines in their spectra, and only later did it become clear that her sequence of letters is a temperature scale. ι Aurigae falls in the class just warmer than the reddest giants, where lines of metals such as iron and calcium grow strong, and that verdict matches the orange your eye reports.

HR8308.question: How hot is the orange star at the nose of Pegasus?
HR8308.why: Between the ruddy and the white corners of Pegasus sits an orange supergiant, the next mark up from the coolest stars.
HR8308.look: Enif marks the nose of the flying horse, west of the Great Square. In binoculars it is a clear orange; compare it with Scheat, the Square's ruddier north-west corner, and with Markab at the corner below.
HR8308.answer: Enif's surface is about 4,200 K, a few hundred degrees warmer than Scheat and still well below the Sun's 5,800 K. That modest gap is why Enif reads orange where Scheat reads orange-red.
HR8308.story: Enif is a supergiant and Scheat a giant, yet the eye sorts them by heat alone, because a star's tint depends on the temperature of its surface and not on how much surface there is. Astronomers tell the two kinds apart in the spectrum instead, where the thin, low-pressure air of a supergiant draws its dark lines unusually sharp.

HR6705.question: Why does Eltanin look orange beside yellow Rastaban in the dragon's head?
HR6705.why: In the dragon's head an orange star and a yellower one sit four degrees apart, so the next steps of the scale arrive in a single sweep.
HR6705.look: From Vega, look about 14° north-west for the four-star head of Draco. Eltanin is the brightest of the four, and in binoculars it is clearly orange while Rastaban, about 4° away, looks yellower.
HR6705.answer: Eltanin's surface is about 4,000 K and Rastaban's about 5,200 K, so the difference you see is more than a thousand degrees. The cooler star glows orange and the warmer one yellow, the order the eye finds everywhere on the scale.
HR6705.story: Eltanin passes almost straight overhead at London, which made it the star James Bradley watched night after night in the 1720s, and its light has been examined closely ever since. Its spectrum says what its color says: strong lines of metals, the first faint bands of the molecules that fill the coolest stars, the signature of a surface roughly a third cooler than the Sun's.

HR7525.question: How can Altair and its orange neighbor Tarazed look so different in one field?
HR7525.why: Aquila packs two marks of the thermometer into one binocular field, and the warmer of the two comes first.
HR7525.look: Put Altair and Tarazed in one field, about 2° apart: crisp white against warm orange. A slight defocus turns them into two small disks and the colors become unmistakable.
HR7525.answer: Tarazed's surface is about 4,200 K and Altair's about 7,600 K, nearly twice as hot, and your eye reads that gap as orange against white. They only look like a pair, since Tarazed lies more than 20 times farther away, but color ignores distance.
HR7525.story: Color ignores distance for a simple reason: as light spreads out across space, every wavelength thins by the same factor, so the proportions of red, green and blue that leave a star are the proportions that reach you. Brightness falls with the square of the distance, but the mixture, which is what the eye reads as color, survives the journey intact.

HR5563.question: Why is one guardian of the pole orange and the other white?
HR5563.why: Near the pole the two guardian stars wear different colors, and the orange one adds the next mark to the scale.
HR5563.look: Between Polaris and the Big Dipper's handle shine the two guardians of the pole. In binoculars Kochab is clearly orange and Pherkad, a few degrees away, white; a touch of defocus makes the colors easier to judge.
HR5563.answer: Kochab is cool enough to glow orange, some 1,700 degrees below the Sun, while Pherkad's white means a much hotter surface. Side by side, the two guardians read as two different marks on the same thermometer.
HR5563.story: Seen from a planet around Kochab, daylight would look distinctly warm, because the star's glow peaks in the near infrared and its visible light is weighted toward red. Our Sun's glow peaks in the middle of the visible range, and eyes that evolved under it read that balanced light as white, so the orange you see in Kochab is a measure of how far its surface falls short of the Sun's.

HR6461.question: Why is β Arae orange when α Arae, six degrees away, is blue-white?
HR6461.why: Low in the southern Milky Way two stars of the Altar make a matched pair of opposites, and the orange one belongs here, one step up from the deep reds.
HR6461.look: Look below the tail of Scorpius, toward the southern horizon. β Arae is a distinctly orange point and α Arae, about six degrees north, is blue-white; the bright globular NGC 6397 lies about three degrees north-east.
HR6461.answer: β Arae's surface is about 4,100 K and α Arae's nearly 22,000 K, more than five times hotter. The orange and the blue-white are those two temperatures, seen side by side.
HR6461.story: Along this stretch of the southern Milky Way, starlight passes through plenty of dust, which steals blue light and could in principle fake an orange tint. Astronomers check for this by comparing a star's color with the temperature its spectral lines give; for β Arae the two largely agree, so its orange is mostly its own.

HR6217.question: How hot is the orange star at the corner of the Southern Triangle?
HR6217.why: The Southern Triangle's brightest corner is also its warmest, the orange mark on a small three-star scale.
HR6217.look: Atria is a vivid orange point at one corner of Triangulum Australe. Defocus slightly to enhance the color, then swing to β, the creamy-white corner, and compare.
HR6217.answer: Atria is nearly 3,000 degrees cooler than β Trianguli Australis, which runs at about 7,200 K, and that is the whole gap between orange and white.
HR6217.story: The brightest corner of the Southern Triangle is its coolest, which shows that brightness and heat are separate questions: a cool star can outshine a hot one simply by having far more surface. Atria gives out thousands of Suns' worth of light from a skin cooler than the Sun's, so it has to be enormous. Its orange tint together with its great output told astronomers it was a giant long before anyone measured its disk.

STAR-Alphard.question: What does the rich orange of Hydra's lonely star say about its heat?
STAR-Alphard.why: In a region almost empty of bright stars, Alphard's orange has nothing to compete with, which makes it an easy step to read.
STAR-Alphard.look: Look about 20 degrees south-west of Regulus for the only bright star in a wide, empty region. In binoculars Alphard is a rich orange; swing to Regulus and back to feel the contrast.
STAR-Alphard.answer: Regulus runs at about 11,500 K, nearly three times Alphard's temperature. An orange tint means a surface cooler than the Sun's, however bright the star looks.
STAR-Alphard.story: Astronomers can read Alphard's temperature from its spectrum as well as its color, and the two must agree for the thermometer to be trusted. In a cool star like this the lines of neutral metals are strong and the hydrogen lines weak, the reverse of a white star. The balance between them changes so steadily with heat that it serves as a second scale beside the color.

HR8502.question: Why is Alpha Tucanae orange, and how hot does that make it?
HR8502.why: In the quiet far south near the Small Magellanic Cloud, an orange giant stands alone and gives the scale its next mark.
HR8502.look: Alpha Tucanae is a soft orange point standing alone in Tucana. Defocus slightly, then sweep about 13° north to blue-white Alnair in Grus and back, and the warm tint holds.
HR8502.answer: Alpha Tucanae's surface runs some 1,600 degrees cooler than the Sun's, the skin of a giant that cooled as it swelled, so its glow tilts toward orange. Alnair, to the north, is about three times hotter.
HR8502.story: A lone star's color is hard to judge, because the eye has nothing to compare it with, and that is why observers sweep from Alpha Tucanae to a hotter neighbor and back. The eye is a poor absolute thermometer but an excellent comparator: set two tints side by side and it ranks them at once, even when it could not have named either one alone.

HR6859.question: Why does one star of the Teapot's spout glow orange?
HR6859.why: The Teapot of Sagittarius doubles as a thermometer, and its orange spout star is the warm mark to begin with.
HR6859.look: Kaus Media is the middle star on the spout side of the Teapot. Defocus slightly to bring out its orange, then drop to blue-white Kaus Australis just below and compare.
HR6859.answer: Its surface is about 4,200 K, while Kaus Australis runs at about 9,500 K, more than twice as hot. The spout's two stars sit far apart on the scale, though only a few degrees apart on the sky.
HR6859.story: The Teapot also shows why astronomers prefer a color they can measure to one they can name. Low in the sky the air itself reddens every star, because a long path through the atmosphere scatters away blue light. The honest comparison is therefore between two stars at the same height, which the spout of the Teapot conveniently provides.

DS-AlmaakDS.question: What temperature lies behind Almach's golden-orange glow?
DS-AlmaakDS.why: Andromeda's chain ends in a golden star, a step warmer in color than the ruddy one at its middle.
DS-AlmaakDS.look: Almach marks the eastern end of Andromeda's chain of bright stars, a golden-orange point in binoculars. Its blue companion is too close to split, so judge the gold against Mirach, the ruddier star in the middle of the chain.
DS-AlmaakDS.answer: Almach's giant runs at about 4,250 K, a few hundred degrees warmer than Mirach, which is enough to turn ruddy into golden. A telescope would show its blue companion at the other end of the scale, but binoculars keep the pair merged and the giant's color wins.
DS-AlmaakDS.story: Why does the giant's color win? Light simply adds, so an unresolved pair reads as the blend of its members weighted by how bright each one is, and here the golden giant gives out far more visible light than its companion. Through a telescope that splits the pair, the companion looks strikingly blue, partly because the eye exaggerates a color contrast when two stars sit side by side.

HR4630.question: Why does Corvus, the crow, have one orange star among its whiter ones?
HR4630.why: The little crow of Corvus holds three marks of the thermometer within a couple of binocular fields, and its orange star comes first.
HR4630.look: Corvus is the small four-star kite south-west of Spica. Minkar is the most orange of its stars; compare it with pale yellow Kraz and blue-white Gienah, each about five degrees away.
HR4630.answer: Kraz runs at about 5,100 K and Gienah at about 12,400 K, so in one small kite the colors climb from Minkar's orange through yellow to blue-white.
HR4630.story: Corvus is a fair test bench, because its tints come from stars at quite different distances and the colors still rank them correctly. Distance dims a star without changing its tint, so the order of colors you see is the order of temperatures, whichever crow star happens to lie nearest.

HR3307.question: How can a blend of two stars still read as orange?
HR3307.why: Orange marks a step up from red, but a star's color can be a blend, and Avior, the warm corner of the False Cross, hides a second star in its light.
HR3307.look: Avior is the brightest star of the False Cross and the only one with a clear orange tint. Compare it with white Aspidiske at the other southern corner of the figure, and defocus slightly to make the difference plain.
HR3307.answer: Its light blends a cool orange giant near 4,300 K with a hot blue companion, and because the giant gives out more visible light, the mixture reads orange. A blended thermometer reading reports mostly the brighter partner.
HR3307.story: Each star's share of a blend depends on which colors you look in. In yellow and red light the cool giant gives out far more, but toward the ultraviolet the hot companion takes over, since a surface as cool as the giant's sends out almost nothing at such short wavelengths. Seen by an ultraviolet camera above the air, the same pair would read as a hot star, so which partner a blend reports depends on the light you collect.

STAR-Arcturus.question: What temperature does the orange-gold of Arcturus stand for?
STAR-Arcturus.why: Orange is the second mark on the scale, and no star shows it more plainly than Arcturus, whose tint is visible even without binoculars.
STAR-Arcturus.look: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle to Arcturus, the brightest star in Boötes. Its orange-gold is obvious in binoculars; carry the same curve on to blue-white Spica and compare.
STAR-Arcturus.answer: Arcturus runs some 1,500 degrees cooler than the Sun, which gives its glow that orange-gold cast. Spica, further along the same curve, burns nearly six times hotter.
STAR-Arcturus.story: Arcturus is poor in iron and the other heavy elements, which makes its air a little more transparent to blue light than a typical giant's. The effect on its tint is small, though, and its orange-gold is overwhelmingly the color of its temperature. Its spectrum has been charted line by line in an atlas so detailed that it serves as the standard against which cool giants everywhere are measured.

HR2553.question: Why does Tau Puppis look warmer in color than Canopus nearby?
HR2553.why: Beside the brilliant white of Canopus sits a modest giant with a warmer tint, and that contrast is the next reading.
HR2553.look: In binoculars Tau Puppis is a soft yellow-orange point. Compare it with brilliant white Canopus about 5° to the west-south-west.
HR2553.answer: Tau Puppis runs roughly 3,000 degrees cooler than Canopus, which shines at about 7,700 K, and that difference shows as yellow-orange against white.
HR2553.story: A star's color comes from the shape of its whole glow, not from any single wavelength, and that shape depends on temperature alone. Tau Puppis and Canopus differ in size, age and power, yet the eye ranks them correctly by heat the moment both are in view, because none of those other differences can bend the balance of red to blue.

HR168.question: Why is Schedar orange when the other stars of the W look white?
HR168.why: Cassiopeia's W is mostly hot white and blue-white stars, and its one warm star gives the scale its orange mark.
HR168.look: Schedar is the bright southern point of Cassiopeia's W. Swing to γ Cassiopeiae at the center of the W and back: orange against blue-white.
HR168.answer: Schedar's surface is about 4,600 K and γ Cassiopeiae's about 28,000 K, roughly six times hotter. The tint reports heat, not power, and Schedar still outshines the Sun hundreds of times over.
HR168.story: Schedar's color also tells part of its life story. A giant like this one was once a hotter, whiter star in its long middle years, and swelling spread the same heat over a much larger surface, so the skin cooled until the eye reads it orange. Among the bright stars of the W it is the one that has moved furthest along that road, and its tint marks how far it has gone.

HR5854.question: What does the pale orange of Unukalhai tell you about its surface?
HR5854.why: Orange comes in shades, and the serpent's heart shows a pale one, close to the point where orange gives way to yellow.
HR5854.look: Unukalhai is the brightest star of Serpens, the serpent's heart. Center it and defocus slightly to bring out its pale orange; the globular cluster M5 lies about eight degrees south-west.
HR5854.answer: Its surface is about 4,500 K, cooler than the Sun but warmer than the deep orange giants, which is why the tint is pale. A few hundred degrees more and it would read yellow.
HR5854.story: Where exactly does orange turn into yellow? There is no sharp line, because the eye blends a smooth spread of colors into one impression, and that impression shifts gradually as the peak of the glow slides out of the infrared toward the visible. Astronomers sidestep the argument by giving each star a number, its color index, and naming the color afterward.

HR6603.question: Why does Cebalrai look orange while Rasalhague, nearby, looks white?
HR6603.why: Ophiuchus offers an orange giant with a white star a short sweep north, so the next step up the scale is never far away.
HR6603.look: In binoculars Cebalrai is clearly orange, with the bright open cluster IC 4665 just north-east of it. Swing about eight degrees north to white Rasalhague and back.
HR6603.answer: Cebalrai's surface is about 4,600 K and Rasalhague's about 7,900 K, and that gap of more than 3,000 degrees is the whole difference between orange and white.
HR6603.story: The orange of Cebalrai and the white of Rasalhague are two points on one smooth curve. Plot how much light a glowing body gives at each color and you get a hump whose peak slides to shorter waves as the temperature rises. Cebalrai's hump peaks in the red, Rasalhague's just beyond the violet, and the eye reads only the part of each hump that falls in its narrow window.

HR4057.question: Why does Algieba shine golden in the mane of Leo?
HR4057.why: Leo's mane glows golden while its heart glows blue-white, and the golden star is the warmer mark to read first.
HR4057.look: Algieba is the brightest star of Leo's Sickle after Regulus. Binoculars cannot split its two golden giants, so judge the merged point: a warm orange-gold, plainly warmer than Regulus at the Sickle's foot.
HR4057.answer: Together they read orange-gold, the color of surfaces about 1,300 degrees cooler than the Sun's. Regulus at the foot of the Sickle runs about two and a half times hotter and glows blue-white for the opposite reason.
HR4057.story: Algieba's two giants differ slightly in tint, the brighter a shade more orange and the fainter a shade more golden, but only a telescope shows them apart. Binoculars hand you their blended light, which is how most stars reach us, as an unresolved sum. Astronomers untangle such sums with spectra, where each star's lines shift back and forth with its orbit and can be assigned to the right partner.

HR617.question: How much cooler is orange Hamal than white Sheratan beside it?
HR617.why: A fair color comparison needs two stars at similar distances, and Aries supplies one, starting with its orange leader.
HR617.look: Hamal leads the short line of Aries, east of the Great Square. In binoculars it is orange; swing to white Sheratan, four degrees south-west, and compare.
HR617.answer: Hamal's surface is about 4,500 K and Sheratan's about 8,150 K, so roughly 3,600 degrees separate orange from white here. Because the two lie at similar distances, dust cannot be faking the difference.
HR617.story: There is a simple rule for where a glow is brightest: divide a fixed number by the temperature and you get the wavelength of the peak, so a hotter body peaks at a shorter, bluer wavelength. For Hamal the arithmetic lands in the red, near 640 nanometers, while for the Sun it lands in the blue-green near 500, which is why Hamal's light leans warm. Wilhelm Wien found the rule in 1893, years before anyone could explain the shape of the whole glow.

HR6241.question: Why does ε Scorpii look paler orange than Antares?
HR6241.why: A modest step in heat should show as a paler tint, and the first bright star of the Scorpion's tail puts that to the test against Antares.
HR6241.look: Drop about nine degrees south-south-east from Antares to the first bright star of the tail. Put each in the field in turn: ε is paler, more yellow-orange, while Antares is a deeper orange-red.
HR6241.answer: ε Scorpii's surface is about 4,500 K, roughly 900 degrees hotter than Antares, so its glow carries more yellow and green and less red. The stars farther down the tail run hotter still.
HR6241.story: Why should the eye notice so modest a difference in heat? At the cool end of the scale the spread of a glow's colors shifts steeply with temperature, and a little extra heat pours in proportionally much more green and blue light than red. At the hot end a far bigger jump changes the tint less, which makes the cool end the easiest part of the thermometer to read.

HR99.question: What makes Ankaa pale orange when Achernar is blue-white?
HR99.why: Between blue-white Achernar and white Fomalhaut stands a lone orange giant, the warm mark against which both can be judged.
HR99.look: Ankaa stands alone between Achernar and Fomalhaut. In binoculars notice its pale orange color, then sweep to blue-white Achernar, about 19 degrees away, and compare.
HR99.answer: Achernar runs at about 14,800 K, more than three times Ankaa's temperature, so the swing between them crosses a long stretch of the thermometer.
HR99.story: This far south the sky holds few bright stars, and both Ankaa and Achernar lie well away from the dusty band of the Milky Way, where the space between the stars is clear. Their light therefore reaches you with its colors untouched, and the warm and bluish tints you compare are the two surfaces as they really are.

HR4301.question: Why is Dubhe yellow-orange when Merak, the other pointer, is white?
HR4301.why: The Big Dipper is a thermometer hiding in plain sight, and its upper pointer star holds the warm end.
HR4301.look: Dubhe is the upper pointer star of the Big Dipper's bowl, and Merak, the lower one, is five degrees away. In binoculars Dubhe is yellow-orange and Merak white, so sweep between them a few times.
HR4301.answer: Dubhe's surface is about 4,700 K and Merak's about 9,500 K, so the two pointers differ by a factor of two in temperature. At the far end of the handle, blue-white Alkaid is hotter still.
HR4301.story: Dubhe and Merak make a clean demonstration that color has nothing to do with brightness, since the two pointers look much alike in brightness and their tints still disagree. Astronomers put numbers on the difference with the color index, a star's brightness through a blue filter minus its brightness through a yellow one. Dubhe's comes out large, while Merak's sits near zero, the mark of a star much like Vega.

HR188.question: Diphda and τ Ceti share a tint, so do they share a temperature?
HR188.why: Color reports temperature, and Cetus offers a test of how far that report goes, with two stars of nearly the same tint.
HR188.look: Diphda is the brightest star of Cetus, alone in a wide, dim region south of Pisces. In binoculars it is yellow-orange; compare it with τ Ceti about fifteen degrees east, which looks a touch paler.
HR188.answer: They nearly do, for Diphda's surface is about 4,850 K and τ Ceti's about 5,300 K, close enough to look alike. Yet Diphda is a giant many times the Sun's width and τ Ceti a dwarf smaller than the Sun, because color reads temperature and nothing about size.
HR188.story: The color reports only the layer that sends out the visible light. Above that skin Diphda wears a corona of thin gas heated to millions of degrees, which radiates about two thousand times as much X-ray power as the Sun's corona, though none of it reaches the eye. So the hottest gas around a star can be the gas you cannot see at all, and the tint is the temperature of the surface, not of everything the star holds.

HR5288.question: Why is Menkent pale orange among the blue-white stars of Centaurus?
HR5288.why: Among the blue-white stars of Centaurus one giant glows warm, and it gives the scale its orange mark.
HR5288.look: Menkent is a pale orange point in binoculars, north of the brilliant stars of Centaurus. Compare it with blue-white Hadar or Spica, each about 25 degrees away, and the warmth of its tint is plain.
HR5288.answer: Its surface is about 4,850 K, a few hundred degrees short of yellow and far below Hadar's roughly 25,000 K. On the thermometer it sits at the warm end of orange.
HR5288.story: The orange of a cool star and the blue-white of a hot one leave fingerprints in their spectra too. In Menkent's light the lines of metals such as iron and calcium are strong, because its gas is cool enough for those atoms to keep their outer electrons. In Hadar's light they nearly vanish and lines of helium appear, which only a far hotter gas can excite.

HR2990.question: How can the twins of Gemini wear such different colors?
HR2990.why: Gemini's twins are a lesson in color, and the warmer twin is where this step of the scale begins.
HR2990.look: Put Pollux and Castor in one field, 4½° apart: Pollux is orange, Castor white, and a touch of defocus makes the difference vivid.
HR2990.answer: Castor runs at about 9,550 K, nearly twice Pollux's temperature, so one twin glows orange and the other white. They are twins in name only, a cool giant beside a hot white star.
HR2990.story: Why are orange giants so common among the bright stars? When a star like Pollux runs out of hydrogen in its core, its outer layers swell, and the same energy spread over a much larger surface leaves each square meter cooler, so a star that was once white settles into orange. Pollux very likely shone white in its youth, much as Castor does now, which makes the twins snapshots of a change in color that comes with age.

HR2773.question: What does the deep orange of Pi Puppis say about its surface?
HR2773.why: Puppis spans the thermometer in a single short sweep, and its deep orange star is the warm mark to start from.
HR2773.look: Pi Puppis glows deep yellow-orange, with a much fainter star just beside it, an easy binocular pair. Defocus slightly and its warmth deepens against the paler stars scattered around it.
HR2773.answer: Its surface is near 3,900 K, about two-thirds of the Sun's, so its glow leans to red and the eye calls it deep orange. Every other bright star in this sweep of Puppis runs hotter, and the scale climbs from here.
HR2773.story: Two stars of the same orange can be very different beasts, and the spectrum tells them apart. The pattern of lines sets the temperature, while their sharpness reveals the pressure in the atmosphere, low in a bloated supergiant and higher in a compact star, and by that reading Pi Puppis is a supergiant. Its glow therefore comes from a surface vastly larger than the Sun's, a cool skin spread wide enough to outshine thousands of Suns.

HR4932.question: How close to the Sun's temperature is Vindemiatrix's pale yellow?
HR4932.why: Halfway up the scale the colors approach the Sun's own, and Virgo's pale yellow giant is the place to see it.
HR4932.look: Vindemiatrix sits in Virgo's northern arm, about 20 degrees west-south-west of Arcturus. In binoculars it is pale yellow; swing to Arcturus and back to see how much warmer orange looks.
HR4932.answer: Vindemiatrix runs some 750 degrees short of the Sun and as much again hotter than Arcturus, which is why it reads yellow where Arcturus reads orange. Spica, blue-white to the south, sits far higher up.
HR4932.story: Between Arcturus and Vindemiatrix the difference in heat is modest, yet the eye sees it at once when the two are compared. Their spectra say the same thing in another language: the cooler star's lines of neutral metals run stronger and the warmer star's weaker, in just the proportion that such a step in heat should produce.

HR6148.question: Why does Kornephoros look yellow beside white Rasalhague?
HR6148.why: Yellow is the Sun's part of the scale, and Kornephoros shows it cleanly, between the orange giants and the white stars around it.
HR6148.look: Kornephoros is a clean yellow point about 10° south of the Keystone of Hercules. Compare its tint with white Rasalhague farther to the south-east, and the yellow becomes obvious.
HR6148.answer: Kornephoros' surface is about 5,100 K, a little cooler than the Sun, while Rasalhague's is about 7,850 K. That gap of nearly 2,800 degrees is the step from yellow to white.
HR6148.story: The kelvin numbers on these cards are anchored, in the end, to the Sun, whose temperature we know better than any other star's. Measure how much sunlight falls on each square meter of Earth, scale it back to the Sun's surface using its size and distance, and only one temperature gives that much light. Stars like Kornephoros are then placed on the same scale by comparing their light with sunlight.

HR6132.question: What does the clean yellow of Eta Draconis mean for its temperature?
HR6132.why: The dragon's body holds a clean yellow giant, the mark where the scale reaches the Sun's own color.
HR6132.look: η Draconis is a clean yellow point in the bend of the dragon's body, between the Big Dipper and the dragon's head. Compare its tint with orange Eltanin in the head, about 16 degrees away, and the difference is one step on the scale.
HR6132.answer: Its surface is about 5,000 K, close to the Sun's 5,800 K and roughly a thousand degrees hotter than Eltanin, which is why it reads yellow instead of orange.
HR6132.story: Why are there no green stars, if the Sun's glow peaks near green? A glowing body never emits a single color; its light is a broad spread, and when the peak sits in the middle of the spectrum the eye mixes everything into white or pale yellow. η Draconis, a little cooler than the Sun, peaks just on the red side of green, enough to tint it yellow.

HR4786.question: Does a star with the Sun's pale yellow have the Sun's temperature?
HR4786.why: In the little crow the middle mark is a pale yellow star, the color of our own Sun.
HR4786.look: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica. In binoculars Kraz is pale yellow, about the Sun's own color; compare it with orange Minkar and blue-white Gienah across the crow.
HR4786.answer: It comes close, for some 700 degrees short of the Sun's surface is near enough for the colors to match. Size is another matter, since Kraz is about 16 times the Sun's width, and color never reports that.
HR4786.story: Kraz shows roughly the color the Sun would have as a point of light at night, a shade warmer. Daylight elsewhere is set the same way: a planet around a cooler star would bask in faintly golden light and one around a hotter star in a whiter light. The eyes of anyone living there would adapt, though, and call their own sunlight plain white.

HR8650.question: Why does Matar look yellow when Scheat, five degrees away, looks orange?
HR8650.why: A notch above ruddy Scheat, a yellow giant in the horse's foreleg holds the Sun's part of the scale.
HR8650.look: Matar lies about five degrees north-west of Scheat, in the foreleg of Pegasus, and binoculars show a yellowish point. Swing to orange Scheat and back to compare.
HR8650.answer: Matar's surface is about 5,000 K and Scheat's about 3,700 K, a difference of some 1,300 degrees that turns orange-red into yellow. A hidden hotter companion adds a little to Matar's light, but the giant sets the color.
HR8650.story: For yellow giants like Matar there is a finer ruler than color. Some dark lines in the spectrum deepen as the gas cools while others barely change, so the ratio of their depths tracks the temperature and can separate stars that differ by a few tens of degrees. The eye could never approach that: it tells Matar's yellow from Scheat's orange at a glance, but it could not rank two stars that close.

HR8232.question: Is the yellow of Sadalsuud really the Sun's color, at the Sun's temperature?
HR8232.why: Aquarius holds a supergiant with the Sun's own tint, the midpoint of the scale where yellow begins.
HR8232.look: Sadalsuud is the brightest star of Aquarius, in a quiet stretch of sky east of Capricornus, and binoculars show a pale yellow point. Sadalmelik, a similar yellow star, lies about ten degrees north-east.
HR8232.answer: Its surface is about 5,500 K, only some 300 degrees below the Sun's, so the tint is genuinely solar. The difference is size, for it is a supergiant about 48 times the Sun's width, and color never tells you that.
HR8232.story: Yellow supergiants are uncommon, because a heavy star tends to pass through this range of temperatures quickly, on its way from hot and blue to cool and red or back again. Catching two of them in Aquarius is a little like finding two travelers in the middle of the same bridge, and their color says where on the crossing each one stands.

HR1829.question: Why does Nihal look yellower than Arneb, its neighbor in the Hare?
HR1829.why: The Hare holds a yellow star and a white one in the same field, and the yellow one comes first.
HR1829.look: Put Nihal and Arneb, the two brightest stars of Lepus below Orion, in the same field, about 3° apart. Arneb looks slightly brighter and whiter, Nihal yellowish.
HR1829.answer: Nihal's surface is about 5,200 K and Arneb's about 7,300 K, so a 2,000-degree difference shows as yellow beside white. That Arneb also looks brighter has nothing to do with color, for it is a far more distant and far more powerful supergiant.
HR1829.story: If Nihal is yellow, what color is the Sun? Seen from space the Sun looks white, because its glow peaks in the middle of the visible range and the eye blends that balanced spread into white. From the ground it looks yellowish because the air scatters away some of its blue. A star a little cooler than the Sun, like Nihal, tips the balance just far enough toward red for the eye to call it yellow at night.

STAR-Capella.question: Why does Capella look yellow, halfway between Rigel's ice and Aldebaran's orange?
STAR-Capella.why: The middle of the scale is the Sun's yellow, and Capella shows it brightly enough that its tint is easy to read.
STAR-Capella.look: Capella is the brilliant star leading the pentagon of Auriga. Sweep to ι Aurigae, the orange star at the pentagon's south-western corner, and back: Capella's creamy, slightly golden tint sits a clear step above that orange, and a slight defocus makes the gold easier to see.
STAR-Capella.answer: Capella is two giants whose surfaces measure about 5,000 and 5,700 K, just below the Sun's 5,800 K, so their blended light is the Sun's own yellow, slightly warmed. Stars clearly whiter than this are hotter than our Sun.
STAR-Capella.story: Capella's two giants have been separated by linked telescopes and measured one at a time, so its blended color can be checked against its parts. The cooler giant leans gold, the warmer one sits nearer the Sun's own tint, and their sum is the creamy yellow you see, a rare case where a star's color can be taken apart and put back together again.

HR509.question: Does a Sun-like star nearby look the Sun's color in binoculars?
HR509.why: To see the Sun's color at night you need a nearby star much like the Sun, and τ Ceti is one.
HR509.look: τ Ceti lies about fifteen degrees east of Diphda, the Whale's brightest star. In binoculars it is a steady pale-yellow point; swing back to Diphda, which looks more orange, to set the two marks on the scale.
HR509.answer: τ Ceti's surface is about 5,300 K, a few hundred degrees below the Sun's, so its pale yellow is very nearly the color of sunlight. Seen from a planet around τ Ceti, our Sun would be a slightly whiter star of the same kind.
HR509.story: τ Ceti is poorer in iron than the Sun, and that matters for its color in a small way, because metals crowd the blue end of a star's spectrum with dark lines. A star with fewer of them lets a little more blue escape and looks a shade whiter than its temperature alone would make it. Astronomers correct for this when they turn colors into temperatures, one reason the thermometer works as well as it does.

HR5459.question: What color is a star with almost exactly the Sun's temperature?
HR5459.why: Every thermometer needs a calibration mark, and the brightest star of Centaurus has a member that is nearly the Sun's twin.
HR5459.look: Find the two Pointers next to the Southern Cross; Alpha Centauri is the one farther from the Cross. Its two Sun-like stars merge into one brilliant point, so compare its warm tint with blue-white Hadar, the other Pointer.
HR5459.answer: Alpha Centauri A runs at about 5,800 K, the Sun's own temperature, and its light looks a warm yellow-white, with its cooler orange partner adding a touch more gold. This is the Sun's color, seen from the outside.
HR5459.story: Alpha Centauri A is so like the Sun that astronomers use it as a laboratory for our own star: its spectrum is almost a copy of sunlight, line for line. Its gentle oscillations, picked up as tiny rhythmic shifts in those lines, weigh it at about a tenth more than the Sun, so the tint you see is carried by a star of very nearly the Sun's build.

HR2693.question: How hot is the creamy-yellow star in Canis Major's triangle?
HR2693.why: Where yellow shades into white, a supergiant in Canis Major sits right on the boundary.
HR2693.look: In Canis Major's triangle south-east of Sirius, Wezen is the creamy-yellow star. Compare it with blue-white Adhara, about 3° away, for a temperature ladder in one sweep.
HR2693.answer: Its surface is about 6,200 K, a little hotter than the Sun, which is why its yellow is pale and creamy. Adhara beside it burns at about 22,000 K, and the gap shows plainly as cream against blue-white.
HR2693.story: For a star as luminous as Wezen, astronomers do not rely on color alone, because its light crosses well over a thousand light-years of space and picks up a little dust on the way. They read the temperature from the ratios of particular dark lines in its spectrum, which dust cannot change, and the result confirms that the creamy tint is very nearly the star's own.

HR7796.question: What color is a star just a little hotter than the Sun?
HR7796.why: At the center of the Northern Cross, amid the Milky Way's crowd of fainter stars, a supergiant shows a tint close to the Sun's.
HR7796.look: Sadr is the star at the center of the Northern Cross. In binoculars it shows a faint yellowish tint against the white Milky Way field; compare it with white Deneb, about 6° to the north-east, and the difference is gentle but real.
HR7796.answer: Sadr's surface is about 6,000 K, just a shade hotter than the Sun's, and at that temperature the eye sees a pale, creamy yellow. Deneb runs some 2,500 degrees hotter and looks white.
HR7796.story: Sadr sits in one of the dustiest stretches of the northern Milky Way, and its light crosses enough of that dust to shift its color slightly toward red. Astronomers measure the shift by comparing the color with the temperature read from its spectral lines; without the dust Sadr would look a touch whiter still, a shade closer to its true place just above the Sun.

HR6212.question: Does a star at the Sun's temperature look yellow or white?
HR6212.why: Hercules holds a nearby star almost exactly as hot as the Sun, the best place in its part of the sky to see what that temperature looks like.
HR6212.look: ζ and η Herculis frame the west side of the Keystone, with the great Hercules globular cluster between them. ζ Her is a simple yellowish point; defocus slightly and compare it with white Vega, about 25° to the east.
HR6212.answer: At about 5,760 K, within a few dozen degrees of the Sun, it looks a soft yellowish white. That is how our Sun would look to someone on a planet circling another star.
HR6212.story: ζ Herculis is a double whose two members circle each other every few decades, and following that orbit gives their masses directly. The brighter one is heavier than the Sun and further along in life, already somewhat swollen, yet its surface happens to sit at almost exactly the Sun's temperature, and temperature is all its color can report.

HR98.question: Is Beta Hydri's soft yellow the same color as our Sun?
HR98.why: Near the south celestial pole shines a Sun-like star whose color you can treat as the Sun's own at night.
HR98.look: Beta Hydri sits near the south celestial pole, roughly between the Small Magellanic Cloud and the pole. Binoculars show a soft yellow star, the tint the Sun would show at night, with the Small Cloud's misty glow about 5° away.
HR98.answer: Its surface is about 5,800 K, matching the Sun's to within a few dozen degrees, so this soft yellow is the Sun's own color seen at night. Anything whiter is hotter than our star, anything more orange cooler.
HR98.story: Beta Hydri is older than the Sun and has begun to swell, yet its surface still sits at the Sun's temperature, because a star in the first stage of growing barely cools. That makes it a preview of the Sun some five billion years from now: the same color, a somewhat larger disk, and the same daylight on whatever worlds it has.

DS-DeltaCep.question: How close to the Sun's own temperature is δ Cephei's yellow?
DS-DeltaCep.why: The yellow mark in Cepheus is an unusual one, because its temperature does not stay put.
DS-DeltaCep.look: δ Cephei marks the south-east corner of the house-shaped figure of Cepheus, a yellowish point with a fainter blue-white companion close beside it. Compare its tint with the Garnet Star, a deep orange-red, about 6° to the west.
DS-DeltaCep.answer: Its surface averages close to the Sun's, swinging between about 5,400 and 6,500 K every 5.37 days, a shift too small for the eye, so the yellow you see is very nearly the Sun's own color.
DS-DeltaCep.story: A light meter fitted with blue and yellow filters catches what the eye misses: through each cycle δ Cephei's color index swings by a few tenths of a magnitude, reddest when the star is dimmest. Color and brightness move together because both are the surface heating and cooling, and that link helped show that a Cepheid's pulse is a real breathing of the star, not a companion passing in front.

HR424.question: What temperature does the North Star's pale yellow stand for?
HR424.why: The North Star is also a mark on the thermometer, a supergiant whose tint sits at the Sun's end of the scale.
HR424.look: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper's bowl up to Polaris. Binoculars show it on a little loop of fainter stars, the Engagement Ring; its pale yellow is subtle, so compare it with orange Kochab, about 16 degrees away.
HR424.answer: Polaris runs at about 6,000 K, a couple of hundred degrees hotter than the Sun, which makes its light a creamy yellow-white. Kochab, at about 4,100 K, shows what nearly 2,000 degrees less looks like.
HR424.story: Polaris pulses, swelling and shrinking slightly every few days, yet its tint never visibly changes, because its temperature swings by only a few tens of degrees, far below anything the eye can detect. Astronomers follow that small swing through the changing strengths of lines in its spectrum, a thermometer far finer than color.

HR5235.question: Why does Muphrid look pale yellow beside orange Arcturus?
HR5235.why: Five degrees from orange Arcturus a paler star waits, the next mark up and a star just beginning to swell.
HR5235.look: Sweep from Arcturus in Boötes about five degrees west to Muphrid. A wide field holds both: orange-gold beside pale yellow-white.
HR5235.answer: Muphrid's surface is about 6,000 K and Arcturus' about 4,300 K, so the step you see is some 1,700 degrees. As Muphrid ages and swells, its surface will cool and its color will slide toward Arcturus' orange.
HR5235.story: Muphrid and Arcturus lie only a few light-years apart, so the light of both crosses the same stretch of nearly empty space, and no dust can favor one tint over the other. That makes the pair a clean bench test: the step from orange-gold to pale yellow is the stars' own, as honest a reading as the sky offers.

HR6536.question: Why does Rastaban look yellower than Eltanin in the dragon's head?
HR6536.why: Four degrees from orange Eltanin, the dragon's head holds a yellower star, the next mark up.
HR6536.look: Sweep from Eltanin to Rastaban, about 4° apart in the head of Draco: orange beside yellow. Defocus a little to make the colors easier to compare.
HR6536.answer: Rastaban's surface is about 5,200 K, over a thousand degrees hotter than Eltanin's, though still a little cooler than the Sun's. It is a giant about forty times the Sun's width, and color reports only the heat.
HR6536.story: The step between the dragon's two eyes is easiest to see with a slight defocus. A sharply focused star is so small that its light falls on only a few of the eye's color-sensing cells and the tint barely registers. Spread it into a small disk and many more of them share the light, so the color has a chance to show.

HR8414.question: How hot is the yellow star beside the Water Jar of Aquarius?
HR8414.why: Beside the Water Jar of Aquarius shines a yellow supergiant, in the Sun's part of the scale.
HR8414.look: Sadalmelik lies in Aquarius about ten degrees north-east of Sadalsuud, and binoculars show a pale yellow point beside the small Y-shaped Water Jar. Compare it with orange Enif, about 11° to the north-west.
HR8414.answer: Sadalmelik's surface is about 5,200 K, roughly 600 degrees cooler than the Sun, so its yellow is a touch warmer than sunlight. Enif, about a thousand degrees cooler again, has crossed into orange.
HR8414.story: Sadalmelik carries the same spectral letter and number as the Sun, G2, yet its surface runs hundreds of degrees cooler. The reason is pressure: in a supergiant's thin, tenuous air, atoms shed electrons more easily, so a cooler gas produces the same pattern of dark lines as the Sun's denser, hotter gas. Color carries no such bias, which is why astronomers read temperature from color and lines together, each one checking the other.

HR1084.question: Does a nearby star smaller than the Sun look warmer in color?
HR1084.why: A small, close neighbor of the Sun shows the yellow part of the scale in its own gentle way.
HR1084.look: From Zaurak, the brightest star of the river west of Rigel, move about 7° west-north-west, past δ Eridani, to the next star of similar brightness; its gentle yellow-orange tint sets it apart. Compare it with white Cursa, near Rigel, to see the next step.
HR1084.answer: Its surface is about 5,100 K, some 700 degrees cooler than the Sun's, so it glows a gentle yellow-orange. Being smaller than the Sun changes its brightness, not its color.
HR1084.story: Why is a star smaller than the Sun also cooler? A lighter star squeezes its core less, burns its fuel more gently and gives out less energy, and that smaller flow of heat leaves its surface cooler and its tint warmer. Among stars in their long, steady middle years, color is therefore a rough guide to weight as well as heat, from hot, heavy white stars down to cool, light orange ones.

HR1605.question: What temperature does ε Aurigae's plain white stand for?
HR1605.why: Above Capella's yellow the scale turns white, and the brightest of the Kids shows the change.
HR1605.look: From Capella, drop a few degrees south to the thin triangle of the Kids; ε Aurigae is the brightest of the three. It is a steady white point, and when you swing back to Capella its yellow looks warmer by comparison.
HR1605.answer: Its surface runs at about 7,300 K, some 1,500 degrees hotter than the Sun's, and at that heat the glow's balance has moved far enough toward blue that the eye calls it white. Capella, at about 5,000 K, still holds on to its yellow.
HR1605.story: When ε Aurigae's dark companion passed in front of it from 2009 to 2011, the star's light fell to less than half, yet its color barely changed. The eclipsing body is a vast disk of dust coarse enough to block every color almost equally, unlike the fine dust between the stars. That gray dimming is one more proof that a star's brightness and its color are separate stories.

HR1017.question: Why does Mirfak look creamy-white when its siblings look blue-white?
HR1017.why: In Perseus a creamy star sits among hotter blue-white siblings, at the place where yellow fades into white.
HR1017.look: Aim at Mirfak, between Capella and Cassiopeia's W, and the field fills with blue-white stars strung in curving chains. Mirfak is a shade yellower than the rest, a creamy white that is easiest to judge with a slight defocus.
HR1017.answer: Mirfak's surface is about 6,350 K, just above the Sun's, while its siblings are much hotter, so its white carries a faint cream tint and theirs a bluish edge. Born the heaviest, it has already swollen and cooled while they have not.
HR1017.story: Siblings share a birthday and a distance, so the cluster around Mirfak is a fair test of the thermometer, with every member's light crossing the same space to reach you. Mirfak's cream against their blue-white is therefore a true difference in surface heat, and spectra confirm it, with Mirfak showing the strong metal lines of a cooler gas and its siblings the helium lines of hotter ones.

STAR-Procyon.question: Why does Procyon look creamy beside icy-white Sirius?
STAR-Procyon.why: Past the Sun the scale turns white, and Procyon shows its first, creamy stage beside the icier white of Sirius.
STAR-Procyon.look: Procyon is the eastern corner of the Winter Triangle, with Sirius and Betelgeuse. Compare it with Sirius to the south and it looks a touch warmer, creamy rather than icy white; then sweep 4° north-west to Gomeisa, bluer still.
STAR-Procyon.answer: Procyon's surface is about 6,600 K and Sirius' about 9,850 K, so the creamy tint is a surface more than 3,000 degrees cooler. Both are hotter than the Sun, which is why neither looks yellow.
STAR-Procyon.story: Procyon looks plainly white on its own and creamy only beside Sirius, because the eye judges a tint mostly by comparison. That is why observers swing between stars: the eye is a poor absolute thermometer but an excellent comparator, and side by side it ranks two whites correctly even when the difference is only a few thousand degrees.

HR6553.question: How hot must Sargas be to look yellow-white amid the blue tail?
HR6553.why: Among the hot blue-white stars of the Scorpion's tail one star looks creamy, the white mark that sits just below them.
HR6553.look: At the lowest point of the tail's curl, Sargas shines yellow-white. Compare it with blue-white Shaula six degrees north: the difference is subtle but real.
HR6553.answer: Sargas runs at about 6,200 K, a few hundred degrees hotter than the Sun, while Shaula burns at about 19,000 K. The two look nearly alike in brightness, so the gentle difference in tint is all temperature.
HR6553.story: In Scorpius the Milky Way is thick with dust, and stars behind it look a little warmer than they are, so astronomers check every color against the spectrum. Sargas passes that test with only a small correction: its yellow-white is mostly its own, the tint of a surface somewhat hotter than the Sun's.

HR7264.question: Why does Albaldah look creamy-white beside blue-white Nunki?
HR7264.why: Above the Teapot's handle a bright giant with a creamy tint sits beside blue-white Nunki, the white step before the hot end.
HR7264.look: Albaldah sits about six degrees north-east of Nunki, above the Teapot's handle. It is a yellow-white point beside blue-white Nunki; defocus slightly and the creaminess shows.
HR7264.answer: Albaldah's surface is about 6,600 K and Nunki's about 18,900 K, nearly three times hotter. Past the Sun's temperature the colors change slowly, so a gap that large shows only as cream against blue-white.
HR7264.story: Albaldah's light reaches us through some of the dust of the Sagittarius Milky Way, which warms its tint slightly. Astronomers measure that warming by comparing the color with the temperature its spectral lines give, and the correction is small enough that the cream you see belongs to the star.

HR21.question: What temperature lies behind Caph's white-yellow glow?
HR21.why: Cassiopeia's western star shows white with a trace of yellow, a mark between the W's orange and blue-white stars.
HR21.look: Caph is the western end of the W of Cassiopeia, a clean white-yellow point. Compare it with orange Schedar, about 5° away, and with blue-white γ Cas at the center of the W.
HR21.answer: Caph's surface runs at about 6,900 K, more than a thousand degrees hotter than the Sun, so its light has lost nearly all its yellow. On the W's own scale it sits between Schedar at about 4,600 K and γ Cassiopeiae at about 28,000 K.
HR21.story: Across the W, Caph also shows how a star's spectrum shifts with heat. Compared with orange Schedar, its metal lines have faded and its hydrogen lines strengthened, while in γ Cassiopeiae lines of helium appear. Three stars of one constellation thus run through the sequence astronomers use to rank temperatures.

HR5897.question: How hot is the creamy-white corner of the Southern Triangle?
HR5897.why: The Southern Triangle's creamy corner sits next to its orange one, so this step of the scale comes with its own comparison.
HR5897.look: Swing between Beta and Atria in Triangulum Australe. Atria looks a little brighter and orange, Beta creamy white.
HR5897.answer: Beta Trianguli Australis runs at about 7,200 K, roughly 3,000 degrees hotter than Atria and 1,400 hotter than the Sun. That is why Beta looks white and Atria orange, though Atria is the more powerful star.
HR5897.story: β Trianguli Australis is in its steady middle years, and stars at that stage follow a simple rule: the hotter are also the heavier, so a white tint marks a star somewhat more massive than the Sun. Atria breaks the rule only because it has left that stage and swollen, which is how a giant can be cool and bright at once.

HR8322.question: What does the white of the Sea Goat's tail say about its temperature?
HR8322.why: At the Sea Goat's tail a nearby star shows the white of a surface hotter than the Sun's.
HR8322.look: Deneb Algedi marks the tail of Capricornus, a white point in binoculars. Compare it with pale yellow Sadalsuud, about 11° to the north, and the step up the scale shows.
HR8322.answer: Deneb Algedi's surface is about 7,300 K, some 1,800 degrees hotter than the yellow supergiant Sadalsuud, which is why it looks white where Sadalsuud looks yellow. Its shallow eclipses dim it slightly from time to time, but the white you see is the hotter star's.
HR8322.story: A surface at Deneb Algedi's temperature sends the peak of its glow to the violet edge of the visible range, so the light you see comes from the downhill side of that peak, slightly richer in blue than in red. That small tilt is what the eye reads as white with no warmth left in it, the first step of the scale above the Sun.

HR591.question: How much hotter than the Sun is the creamy star of Hydrus?
HR591.why: Hydrus holds a Sun-like star and a hotter, creamier one, and this is the creamier, the white step just below the hot end.
HR591.look: Put Achernar and Alpha Hydri in the same sweep, about 5° apart. Achernar looks icy blue-white, Alpha Hydri slightly warmer and creamier.
HR591.answer: Alpha Hydri runs some 1,300 degrees hotter than the Sun and its Sun-like neighbor Beta Hydri, enough to drain the yellow and leave only a hint of cream. Achernar, 5° away, runs roughly twice as hot and looks icy.
HR591.story: Alpha Hydri's creamy white belongs to a surface about a quarter hotter than the Sun's, and that modest step changes daylight more than its tint suggests. A planet around it would receive noticeably more ultraviolet, because a glow's output at short wavelengths climbs steeply with temperature. The eye sees just the last of the cream draining away, while a sunburn would tell the difference fast.

HR7557.question: How hot is Altair, the white star of the Eagle?
HR7557.why: Altair's white is the mark above the Sun on the scale, and orange Tarazed two degrees away makes it easy to read.
HR7557.look: Binoculars fit Altair into one field with its two attendants, orange Tarazed about 2° to one side and fainter Alshain on the other, a short straight line that marks the eagle. Tarazed's warm tint is easy to see, and beside it Altair stays crisp white.
HR7557.answer: Altair averages about 7,600 K, though its fast spin leaves the poles near 8,450 K and the equator near 6,900 K, so one star spans part of the white range by itself. All of it is well above the Sun's 5,800 K, which is why it looks white.
HR7557.story: Altair is close and bright enough that its spectrum has been measured in exquisite detail. The strength of its hydrogen lines sits a little below their peak, the mark of a surface somewhat cooler than the hottest white stars. Its spin, which leaves its poles hotter than its waist, also smears every line, a reminder that one star can hold a small range of temperatures.

HR8162.question: What does Alderamin's clean white say about its temperature?
HR8162.why: Cepheus holds both the deep red of the Garnet Star and a clean white star five degrees away, the next mark up.
HR8162.look: Alderamin is the bright corner of Cepheus nearest Cygnus, a clean white point in binoculars. Sweep about 5° south-east to the Garnet Star and back, and the contrast spans most of the scale.
HR8162.answer: Alderamin's surface is about 7,500 K, hotter than the Sun by some 1,700 degrees and twice as hot as the Garnet Star. Its fast spin leaves the equator cooler than the poles, but from here the blend reads plain white.
HR8162.story: Alderamin and the Garnet Star show how wide the eye's thermometer really is: one tint is white, the other deep red, and between them lie all the orange and yellow stars of the night. The color index measures a star's brightness through a blue filter minus its brightness through a yellow one. On that scale the Garnet Star sits near the red extreme of everything binoculars can show, and Alderamin close to the neutral middle.

HR1865.question: How hot is the white supergiant of Lepus?
HR1865.why: In the Hare a white supergiant stands one notch above the yellow star beside it.
HR1865.look: Find Lepus, the Hare, below Rigel and Saiph. Arneb is its brightest star, white beside yellowish Nihal about 3° away, and Rigel above shows the next color up.
HR1865.answer: Arneb's surface is about 7,300 K, roughly 2,000 degrees hotter than Nihal and 1,500 hotter than the Sun. Its great brightness comes from size and power, but its whiteness comes from heat alone.
HR1865.story: Arneb's light crosses more than two thousand light-years, yet its white arrives nearly intact, because it lies well below the dusty plane of the Milky Way, where the space between the stars is clean. Astronomers check this by comparing its color with the temperature its spectrum gives, and for Arneb the two agree within a small margin.

HR3699.question: Why is Aspidiske white while Avior, across the False Cross, is orange?
HR3699.why: The False Cross has a warm corner and a white one, and this is the white.
HR3699.look: Aspidiske marks one corner of the False Cross. Compare its white with Avior's orange, about 7° away at the other southern corner of the figure.
HR3699.answer: Aspidiske's surface is about 7,100 K and Avior's cool giant about 4,300 K, so the False Cross holds a span of some 2,800 degrees between two corners. Your eye sees it as white against orange.
HR3699.story: Aspidiske is a supergiant, and supergiants are harder to place by eye alone, because their thin, extended atmospheres draw sharp spectral lines unlike those of ordinary white stars. Astronomers read its temperature from the balance of hydrogen and metal lines, and the result sits comfortably above the Sun's, as the eye's verdict of white suggests.

DS-AlpLib.question: What temperature does the white of Libra's brightest star stand for?
DS-AlpLib.why: Libra's brightest star is white, with a creamier companion that binoculars split easily.
DS-AlpLib.look: Find Libra between Spica and Antares. Center Zubenelgenubi and look just north-west for its fainter companion, easy even at 7×: the bright star is white, the companion a touch creamier.
DS-AlpLib.answer: The bright star's surface is about 8,100 K, some 2,300 degrees hotter than the Sun, and its companion's creamier tint hints at a slightly cooler surface. Two stars that travel together still each carry their own temperature.
DS-AlpLib.story: A wide pair that travels together is a gift for the color thermometer, because both stars sit at the same distance behind the same dust, so any difference in tint is theirs alone. Here the brighter star is also the hotter, the usual rule for two stars in their steady middle years: the heavier one burns hotter and shines brighter at once.

HR2326.question: Why does Canopus shine white rather than yellow like the Sun?
HR2326.why: Past the Sun the scale turns white, and the brilliant star south of Sirius shows it best when it stands high.
HR2326.look: Canopus is the brilliant star well south of Sirius. Low in the sky our air splits its light into flickering colors, while higher up it shows a steady white.
HR2326.answer: Its surface is about 7,700 K, some 1,900 degrees hotter than the Sun's, and at that heat the glow's balance has shifted far enough toward blue that the eye sees white. The flashes of red and green near the horizon belong to our atmosphere, not to the star.
HR2326.story: Astronomers measure colors against a reference: by convention a star like Vega has a color index of zero, so cooler stars come out positive and hotter ones negative.
