Canopus lands just on the positive side, the mark of a white star a little cooler than Vega, which is exactly the faint warmth it shows beside icier Sirius.

HR6556.question: How much hotter is white Rasalhague than orange-red Rasalgethi beside it?
HR6556.why: Five degrees apart in Ophiuchus sit a white star and an orange-red one, and the white one is the reading here.
HR6556.look: Swing between Rasalhague and Rasalgethi: white against orange-red, obvious even to the naked eye once you compare them, and deeper in binoculars.
HR6556.answer: Rasalgethi runs at about 3,300 K, less than half Rasalhague's temperature, a gap your eye reads instantly as white against orange-red.
HR6556.story: Rasalhague spins fast enough to flatten itself, and a squashed star is hotter at its poles than at its stretched waist, by more than a thousand degrees in this case. Its color is therefore an average over a surface of several temperatures, still white everywhere, but varied enough for the finest instruments to map.

HR1666.question: How hot is Cursa, the white star beside Orion's foot?
HR1666.why: Beside Orion's foot a nearby white star sits just below blue-white Rigel on the scale.
HR1666.look: Find Rigel and look about 3° north-west for a fainter white star: Cursa. Compare the two in one field; Cursa's white is a little softer, Rigel's a little bluer.
HR1666.answer: Cursa's surface is about 8,400 K and Rigel's about 12,100 K, yet that gap of 3,700 degrees makes only a slight difference in tint. Past white, the colors change slowly even when the temperatures change a lot.
HR1666.story: Cursa's spectrum is dominated by the dark lines of hydrogen, which reach their greatest strength in white stars of about this kind. Hydrogen absorbs those colors only when its electron sits one step up from the bottom, which takes a gas hot enough to lift it there but not so hot that it tears the electron away. The strength of the lines is therefore itself a thermometer, peaking among the white stars.

HR403.question: How hot is Ruchbah, the white star in Cassiopeia's W?
HR403.why: In Cassiopeia's W a white star sits between the orange of Schedar and the blue-white of γ Cassiopeiae.
HR403.look: Ruchbah is the fourth star of the W, counting from Caph. It looks white, much like γ Cas next door; defocus both and γ shows a slightly bluer edge.
HR403.answer: Ruchbah runs at about 7,800 K, some 2,000 degrees hotter than the Sun, against roughly 28,000 K for γ Cassiopeiae. Though γ is more than three times hotter, the two whites differ only slightly, because the eye's color scale flattens at the hot end.
HR403.story: Why does the eye flatten the hot end? Color vision works by comparing how strongly three kinds of cone cells respond. Once a star's glow peaks beyond violet, the visible part keeps nearly the same balance among the three, even as the star's total output soars into the ultraviolet. Ruchbah and γ Cassiopeiae differ enormously in heat but only slightly in that balance.

HR553.question: Why do two stars at nearly the same distance show such different colors?
HR553.why: Aries holds a white star at nearly the same distance as orange Hamal, which makes their color difference a clean test.
HR553.look: Sheratan sits in the short line of Aries, a white point in binoculars. Swing to Hamal, about four degrees north-east, and compare: white against orange.
HR553.answer: Sheratan's surface is about 8,150 K, nearly twice Hamal's 4,500 K, and with distance and dust ruled out, that gap is the whole reason for the colors. You are seeing two temperatures side by side.
HR553.story: Sheratan is really two stars, far too close for any eyepiece to split, but the Mark III interferometer on Mount Wilson resolved them and followed their eccentric orbit of about 107 days, which weighs both. The white star comes out at about twice the Sun's mass and its partner at almost exactly one Sun, with a surface very like the Sun's own. One point of light thus holds a measured case of the rule that among stars in their prime the heavier is the hotter.

HR4357.question: What does Zosma's white say about the heat of its surface?
HR4357.why: On the lion's back a white star sits between golden Algieba and blue-white Regulus, the next mark up.
HR4357.look: Zosma and its neighbor Chertan form the lion's back in Leo, with Denebola at the tail. In binoculars Zosma is white; compare it with golden Algieba in the mane.
HR4357.answer: Zosma runs some 2,400 degrees hotter than the Sun and nearly twice as hot as Algieba, so the gold of the mane gives way to white on the back. Regulus, hotter again, adds a blue edge.
HR4357.story: A surface as hot as Zosma's sends the peak of its glow into the ultraviolet, beyond violet, so even the visible light you see is tilted slightly toward blue. The Sun's peak sits in the middle of the visible range, which the eye reads as neutral, and between the two peaks lies the whole step from the gold of the lion's mane to the white of its back.

STAR-Fomalhaut.question: What temperature does Fomalhaut's lonely white glow stand for?
STAR-Fomalhaut.why: Alone in its part of the sky, Fomalhaut has no rival for attention, so its white is easy to judge on its own.
STAR-Fomalhaut.look: Follow the western side of the Great Square of Pegasus, from Scheat through Markab, and keep going about 45 degrees south. Fomalhaut is the only bright star in that part of the sky, a clean white in binoculars.
STAR-Fomalhaut.answer: Its surface is about 8,600 K, some 2,800 degrees hotter than the Sun's, so its glow is balanced enough to look white. Orange Ankaa, about 22° to the south-east, has a surface about half as hot.
STAR-Fomalhaut.story: Fomalhaut's spectrum is dominated by strong lines of hydrogen, and their strength is a thermometer of its own. Hydrogen can absorb those colors only when its electron has been lifted one step up, which needs a hot gas but not too hot a one, so the lines are strongest in white stars and fade toward both ends of the scale.

HR1713.question: How much hotter than Betelgeuse is the blue-white foot of Orion?
HR1713.why: The hot end of Orion's thermometer sits diagonally across the figure from Betelgeuse, so the whole scale fits inside one constellation.
HR1713.look: Rigel is Orion's foot, the brilliant blue-white star diagonally across from Betelgeuse. Hold it in the field and its icy color is unmistakable, especially just after a look at the orange shoulder.
HR1713.answer: Rigel's surface is about 12,100 K, more than three times Betelgeuse's and twice the Sun's. At that heat much of its glow pours out as ultraviolet, and the visible part we catch is tilted toward blue.
HR1713.story: Rigel's spectrum shows faint lines of helium, an element so reluctant to absorb light that only a very hot gas can make it do so. Those lines alone place Rigel above the white stars, a temperature reading that does not depend on its color at all, and they grow stronger in the hotter stars of Orion's Belt.

HR1790.question: Why is Orion's western shoulder blue-white while the eastern one is orange?
HR1790.why: Orion's western shoulder mirrors Betelgeuse across the hunter, but not on the thermometer.
HR1790.look: Put Bellatrix in the field, then swing about 7° across to Betelgeuse: blue-white against orange. Betelgeuse is usually the brighter, but brightness does not set color, so the difference you read is temperature.
HR1790.answer: Bellatrix's surface is about 22,000 K, roughly six times Betelgeuse's 3,600 K, and that gap is the whole difference between blue-white and orange. The two shoulders are neighbors in the figure and almost opposite ends of the thermometer.
HR1790.story: A star as hot as Bellatrix sends most of its energy out as ultraviolet light, which no eye can see and our atmosphere blocks. Telescopes flown above the air were needed to measure that hidden output, and only once it was counted did the true power of such stars, and their temperatures, fall into place.

HR1903.question: How hot is the middle star of Orion's Belt?
HR1903.why: The middle of Orion's Belt is a blue supergiant, and it shows how hot the hot end can get.
HR1903.look: Center the middle Belt star and let the other two sit near the field edges. All three are blue-white, and the curving string of fainter stars around them shares the same steely tint.
HR1903.answer: Alnilam runs at more than four times the Sun's temperature, yet it looks hardly bluer than Rigel at half that heat, because at the hot end of the scale the visible color barely changes.
HR1903.story: Alnilam's temperature comes from the balance of lines in its spectrum, because the hotter a gas, the more of each kind of atom loses electrons. The ratio of lines from atoms in different states works like a set of thermometer marks far beyond the reach of color. Meghnad Saha worked out the rule behind this in 1920, and it is how astronomers first turned spectral classes into temperatures.

HR2004.question: Why does Saiph look no bluer than Rigel, though it is twice as hot?
HR2004.why: The hot end of the scale hides a surprise, and Orion's second foot shows where the eye's thermometer starts to run out of range.
HR2004.look: Compare Saiph with Rigel at Orion's opposite foot. Both are blue-white, Rigel brighter, and nothing in the tint tells you which is hotter.
HR2004.answer: Saiph's surface is about 26,500 K, more than twice Rigel's, yet both send the eye the same blue-white tail of their glow. Past this point the eye's thermometer saturates: it can say hot, but no longer how hot.
HR2004.story: A star as hot as Saiph pours out most of its energy as ultraviolet light, invisible to the eye and stopped by our atmosphere, so its full power could only be counted once telescopes rose above the air. What reaches your eye is the faint blue-tilted edge of that output, the same edge any very hot star shows.

HR1879.question: How hot is the star at the center of Orion's head?
HR1879.why: At Orion's head, inside a young cluster, shines a star of the hottest class, a test for any thermometer.
HR1879.look: Point at Orion's head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix. Binoculars turn the faint naked-eye smudge into a compact triangle of blue-white stars with a dozen fainter ones around it.
HR1879.answer: Meissa's surface is about 35,000 K, roughly six times the Sun's temperature and ten times Betelgeuse's, yet its color is the same steely blue-white as stars a third as hot. At this end of the scale a spectrum, not the eye, reads the temperature.
HR1879.story: Meissa belongs to the hottest class of stars, recognized by lines of helium that has lost one of its two electrons, a state only extreme heat can keep up. The strength of those lines, not the color, is how astronomers know it runs hotter than even the blue-white supergiants of Orion's Belt below it.

HR1791.question: Why does Elnath look blue-white across the pentagon from orange ι Aurigae?
HR1791.why: The Auriga pentagon closes at a blue-white star, the hot end of a small scale that also holds orange, yellow and white.
HR1791.look: Elnath completes the Auriga pentagon and also marks the tip of the Bull's northern horn. Compare its blue-white with orange ι Aurigae, about 8° across the pentagon.
HR1791.answer: Elnath's surface is about 13,600 K, more than three times ι Aurigae's, so its light is tilted toward blue. Around one small pentagon you can read four steps of the scale.
HR1791.story: Beyond white, the eye's thermometer flattens. A star this hot peaks in the ultraviolet, and the visible part of its glow is the gently sloping tail of that peak, which looks much the same blue-white whether the star is twice the Sun's temperature or five times. That is why Elnath and ι Aurigae differ so plainly, while Elnath and far hotter stars look nearly alike.

HR1165.question: Why do all the bright Pleiades share the same blue-white color?
HR1165.why: The Pleiades are a family of hot young stars, and their brightest member shows the hot end of the scale.
HR1165.look: Center the Pleiades and find Alcyone, the brightest point near the middle. Every bright member shares its blue-white color; compare the whole group with orange Aldebaran, about 14° to the south-east.
HR1165.answer: Alcyone's surface is about 13,500 K, more than three times Aldebaran's, and its bright sisters are hot young stars too, all born together about 125 million years ago. A shared color here means a shared range of temperature, set by a shared youth.
HR1165.story: In long-exposure photographs the Pleiades sit in a blue haze, which is dust reflecting their light. Dust scatters blue light more readily than red, so the haze looks bluer than the stars themselves, by the same physics that makes the daytime sky blue. It is the reverse of the reddening a star suffers when seen straight through dust.

STAR-Sirius.question: What temperature makes Sirius blaze such a pure, icy-looking white?
STAR-Sirius.why: The brightest star of the night sky sits at the top of the white range, where white begins to take on a bluish edge.
STAR-Sirius.look: Orion's Belt, followed down and to the left, points straight at Sirius. Low in the sky it flickers red, green and blue, but that is our air; park it near the edge of the field and its steady color is a crisp, slightly bluish white.
STAR-Sirius.answer: Sirius burns at about 9,850 K, some 4,000 degrees hotter than the Sun, enough to tip its glow toward blue without making it truly blue. That faintly icy white is what a surface near 10,000 K looks like.
STAR-Sirius.story: The faint companion that circles Sirius is hotter still, a white dwarf whose surface runs more than twice as hot as Sirius itself. Yet it is lost in the glare, because a surface the size of Earth sheds little light however hot it is. Could you see it on its own, its tint would be bluer than its brilliant partner's, a vivid reminder that color reports heat and brightness reports something else entirely.

HR2618.question: Why does Adhara look bluer than Sirius, though fainter?
HR2618.why: In the triangle south-east of Sirius a fainter star waits, a test of whether brightness or color is the better guide to heat.
HR2618.look: Find the triangle of bright stars south-east of Sirius; Adhara is the westernmost and brightest of them. Compare its blue-white with Sirius' whiter glare and with creamy Wezen beside it.
HR2618.answer: Adhara's surface is about 22,000 K, more than twice Sirius', so its glow leans further toward blue. It looks fainter only because of distance, and distance never changes a color.
HR2618.story: Adhara is the brightest source in the sky of extreme ultraviolet light, the hard, short-wave radiation that hot stars pour out and that the hydrogen between the stars normally swallows. Toward Adhara a tunnel of thin gas lets it through, and satellites above the air found it outshining every other star at those wavelengths, a direct glimpse of the hidden glow its blue-white tint only hints at.

HR2294.question: How hot is Mirzam, the blue-white star that rises before Sirius?
HR2294.why: Five degrees from Sirius rises a fainter star with a bluer cast, the hot end of the scale in Canis Major.
HR2294.look: Look about 5° west of Sirius for a blue-white star: Mirzam. Compare the two and Sirius looks dazzling, Mirzam modest, with a slightly bluer tint.
HR2294.answer: Mirzam's surface is about 25,300 K, two and a half times as hot as Sirius, which tips its tint slightly toward blue. Its modest brightness is a matter of distance, which dims a star without touching its tint.
HR2294.story: Most of Mirzam's energy leaves as ultraviolet, invisible to the eye and blocked by our air, so its full output was only counted once telescopes flew above the atmosphere. That hidden light is why a star with a modest blue-white tint can be tens of thousands of times more powerful than the Sun.

HR2891.question: What temperature gives Castor its clean white, beside orange Pollux?
HR2891.why: Gemini's white twin, four and a half degrees from its orange brother, sits near the top of the white range.
HR2891.look: Compare Castor's white with Pollux's orange, 4½° away. At 10× Castor looks single, because its two bright stars sit only 5 arcseconds apart, and their light merges into one white point.
HR2891.answer: Castor's surface runs at about 9,550 K, nearly twice Pollux's temperature, so the twins sit far apart on the scale. Castor's six stars blend into that single reading, which its bright white pairs dominate.
HR2891.story: Castor's two bright stars sit close to the temperature at which hydrogen's dark lines are strongest. Those lines need hydrogen atoms whose electron has been lifted one step up but not torn away, and that balance is best struck in white stars like these. In cooler stars too few atoms are lifted, and in hotter ones too many are stripped bare.

HR2088.question: Why does Menkalinan look whiter than Capella at the top of the pentagon?
HR2088.why: Menkalinan is the white mark of Auriga's scale, one step below blue-white Elnath.
HR2088.look: Find the Auriga pentagon, with Capella at its top; Menkalinan is the white star at its eastern corner, about 8° from Capella. Swing between them: cream-gold against white.
HR2088.answer: Menkalinan's two stars have surfaces near 9,000 K, nearly twice Capella's, and at that heat the glow loses its gold. Its eclipses dim it a little but are far too slight for the eye.
HR2088.story: Twin stars make good thermometers. When two stars of the same temperature eclipse each other, the dips come out equally deep, because the light lost depends on how brightly each square meter of the hidden surface shines. Menkalinan's dips match closely. That confirms that both stars share one temperature, so the white you see is that temperature with no blend to untangle.

HR2845.question: Why does Gomeisa look bluer than Procyon right beside it?
HR2845.why: Four degrees from creamy Procyon sits a star with a bluer tint, the hot end of the scale in Canis Minor.
HR2845.look: Put Procyon and Gomeisa, in the little constellation Canis Minor, in one sweep and compare colors: Procyon is creamy white, Gomeisa bluer.
HR2845.answer: Gomeisa's surface is about 11,800 K and Procyon's about 6,600 K, so the hotter star's glow leans toward blue. Procyon only looks brighter because it is about fourteen times closer.
HR2845.story: Beyond white, the eye's thermometer flattens: a star hotter than this peaks in the ultraviolet, and the part of its glow the eye can see is a gently sloping tail that changes little as the temperature climbs. Gomeisa sits just past that bend, hot enough to look bluer than Procyon, and far hotter stars would look to you almost exactly like it.

HR3982.question: What temperature does the blue-white heart of Leo stand for?
HR3982.why: Leo's heart glows blue-white where its mane glows golden, and the heart is the hot end.
HR3982.look: Regulus is the bright dot at the bottom of the backward question mark of Leo's head, crisp and blue-white in binoculars. Swing up the Sickle to golden Algieba and back.
HR3982.answer: Regulus runs at about 11,500 K, roughly twice the Sun's temperature and two and a half times Algieba's, so Leo's brightest star looks steely where its mane looks warm. Its fast spin leaves the equator cooler than the poles, a small spread inside one reading.
HR3982.story: On the astronomers' color index Regulus comes out slightly negative, meaning it is a little brighter in blue light than in yellow, the reverse of every cooler star in Leo. That small minus sign is all the eye's blue-white amounts to, and it shows how compressed the hot end really is: Regulus and stars several times hotter differ in color index by only a few tenths.

HR5056.question: How hot is Spica, the blue-white star at the end of the arc from Arcturus?
HR5056.why: The arc that starts at orange Arcturus ends at a lone blue-white star, the hot end of the scale in Virgo.
HR5056.look: From Arcturus, continue the Dipper-handle curve about as far again to a lone, brilliant blue-white star. Compare its icy color with Arcturus' orange.
HR5056.answer: Spica's main star runs at about 25,300 K, nearly six times Arcturus' temperature, and most of what it gives off is ultraviolet your eyes cannot see. The blue-white that does reach you is just the long-wavelength edge of its glow.
HR5056.story: Spica's two stars orbit too closely to separate, but each leaves its own lines in the spectrum, shifting back and forth with the orbit, so astronomers can read two temperatures from one point of light. Both are hot, the brighter more so, and their blend is the icy blue-white you see.

HR4662.question: Why does Gienah look blue-white when its crow-mates are orange and yellow?
HR4662.why: The little crow's thermometer finishes with a crisp blue-white star.
HR4662.look: Find Corvus, the small kite of stars south-west of Spica. In binoculars Gienah is crisply blue-white; swing to orange Minkar or pale yellow Kraz to compare.
HR4662.answer: Gienah runs at roughly twice the Sun's temperature and nearly three times Minkar's, so its glow tips toward blue. Within one small kite of stars you have read three marks of the scale.
HR4662.story: Among stars still burning hydrogen in their cores, surface heat follows weight, and Gienah's blue-white goes with a star of about four Suns. Such a star shines some three hundred times as brightly as the Sun and spends its fuel to match, so Gienah is only about 160 million years old, born while dinosaurs walked the Earth. Read this way, a tint is a rough scale and a clock as well as a thermometer.

HR5685.question: Why do some observers swear Zubeneschamali looks green?
HR5685.why: Libra's second star is famous for a color the thermometer says no star can have.
HR5685.look: Center Zubeneschamali and defocus slightly so it becomes a small disk. Compare it with white Zubenelgenubi nine degrees south-west and decide for yourself: green tinge, pale blue, or plain white?
HR5685.answer: Its surface is about 12,300 K, which places it among the blue-white stars and nowhere near a green. The green some observers report comes from contrast with nearby colors and from the way our eyes handle dim light, not from the star.
HR5685.story: Color scientists can plot every tint the human eye can perceive on a single chart, and the colors of glowing bodies at every temperature trace one curved track across it. The track runs from deep red through orange, yellow and white to a pale sky blue, and it never enters the green part of the chart at all. Put Zubeneschamali's temperature on that track and it lands among the pale blue-whites, the tint shown on its swatch.

DS-AlpCVn.question: How hot is Cor Caroli, the blue-white star below the Dipper's handle?
DS-AlpCVn.why: A short sweep from La Superba, one of the reddest stars in the sky, shines a crisp blue-white star that closes the scale.
DS-AlpCVn.look: Cor Caroli is the brightest star below the Big Dipper's handle, a crisp blue-white in binoculars. About 7° to the north, toward Megrez, La Superba glows red-orange for contrast.
DS-AlpCVn.answer: Cor Caroli's surface is about 12,000 K, roughly twice the Sun's temperature and more than four times La Superba's, which is why the two look like ice and ember in neighboring fields.
DS-AlpCVn.story: Why does a star this hot look only blue-white and not deep blue? Its glow peaks far into the ultraviolet, and the narrow window the eye can see catches only the long tail of that glow, which slopes gently toward blue whatever the exact temperature. So the eye tells Cor Caroli from La Superba at a glance, but it would struggle to tell it from a star twice as hot.

HR5793.question: What temperature does the white jewel of the Northern Crown stand for?
HR5793.why: The one bright jewel of the Northern Crown is a white mark on the scale, a sweep east of orange Arcturus.
HR5793.look: Alphecca is the one bright star in the arc of Corona Borealis, and binoculars fit the whole crown into one or two fields. It is a clean white, perhaps with a faint bluish edge; compare it with orange Arcturus, about 20° to the west.
HR5793.answer: Alphecca's surface runs at about 9,700 K, more than twice Arcturus' temperature, so its light leans to blue where Arcturus leans to orange. A smaller Sun-like companion hides in the glare, but the hot star sets the color.
HR5793.story: Alphecca sits almost exactly where Vega does on the astronomers' color scale, whose zero point was chosen so that stars of this kind come out neutral. Warmer stars such as Arcturus get positive numbers and hotter blue-white ones negative, so the scale's zero falls right at the jewel you are looking at.

HR5191.question: Why is the end of the Big Dipper's handle blue-white while Dubhe glows orange?
HR5191.why: The Big Dipper's handle ends at its hottest star, the opposite end of the figure from yellow-orange Dubhe.
HR5191.look: Alkaid ends the Big Dipper's handle, crisply blue-white against yellow-orange Dubhe at the far end of the bowl. Sweep from one to the other through the white stars between.
HR5191.answer: Dubhe, at about 4,700 K, is nearly four times cooler, so the Dipper runs from orange to blue-white across one familiar shape. Most of the white stars between them sit near 9,500 K, a middle mark on the same scale.
HR5191.story: A hotter surface pays off steeply in light: the glow from each square meter climbs with the fourth power of the temperature, so doubling the heat multiplies it sixteen times. Each patch of Alkaid's surface therefore outshines an equal patch of the Sun nearly a hundredfold, and although the star is only a few times the Sun's width, it pours out hundreds of Suns' worth of light. Its tint is a measure of its power too, once you know its size.

STAR-Vega.question: Why does Vega look faintly blue, and how hot does that make it?
STAR-Vega.why: Vega is the white mark of Lyra, the brightest star in its part of the sky, where its bluish white stands out against warmer neighbors.
STAR-Vega.look: Vega is the jewel of Lyra. In binoculars it is a hard white spark with a faint blue cast; compare it with orange-red δ² Lyrae, about 4° away, to see most of the scale in one small constellation.
STAR-Vega.answer: Vega's surface is a little over one and a half times as hot as the Sun's, enough to tip the glow just past white toward blue. That faint blue cast is where white starts to shade into the hot end.
STAR-Vega.story: Vega is the star astronomers built their brightness and color scales around. By long convention its magnitude is close to zero, and its color index, the difference between its brightness in blue and yellow light, is set to zero. Every other star's color is measured against it, so when you judge Vega's faint blue you are looking at the scale's own zero mark.

HR7528.question: How hot is the white star at the tip of the Northern Cross?
HR7528.why: The arm of the Northern Cross ends at a white star with a bluish edge, the top of the white range in Cygnus.
HR7528.look: Al Fawaris is the bright star at the end of the western arm of the Northern Cross, white with a faint bluish edge. Compare it with yellowish Sadr, about 8° away at the center of the cross.
HR7528.answer: Al Fawaris runs at about 10,150 K, while Sadr, at the center of the cross, is some 4,000 degrees cooler and holds a cream tint, so one arm of the cross spans the step from yellow to white.
HR7528.story: Stars near Al Fawaris's temperature sit at the upper edge of the white stars for a physical reason. Around this heat the gas is hot enough for hydrogen's dark lines to be at their strongest, while the lines of helium, which need more heat still, have barely begun to show. Hotter stars bring helium in, and with it the bluish edge of the next step.

HR7235.question: How hot is the white star at the Eagle's tail?
HR7235.why: At the eagle's tail a star a step above white Altair tops the white range in Aquila.
HR7235.look: Deneb el Okab is a clean white point about 12° west-north-west of Altair, at the eagle's tail. Compare it with orange Tarazed for a quick color lesson.
HR7235.answer: Deneb el Okab's surface is about 9,200 K, some 1,600 degrees hotter than Altair, which leaves its white a shade bluer. Tarazed, at about 4,200 K, shows the warm end of the same constellation.
HR7235.story: Astronomers measure colors against a reference: by convention a star like Vega has a color index of zero, cooler stars come out positive and hotter ones negative. Deneb el Okab sits almost exactly on that zero, the mark of a star near the top of the white range, while orange Tarazed in the same constellation lands far up the positive side.

HR8238.question: How hot is Alfirk, the blue-white star of Cepheus?
HR8238.why: Cepheus holds one of the reddest stars in the sky, and also a blue-white one to close the scale.
HR8238.look: β Cephei lies in Cepheus between Alderamin and Errai, and binoculars show a blue-white point. Sweep about 12° south to the Garnet Star and back for the full span of the scale.
HR8238.answer: Alfirk's surface is about 27,000 K, more than seven times the Garnet Star's temperature, yet it looks only blue-white, not deep blue. At such heat most of its glow is ultraviolet, and the eye sees only the edge of it.
HR8238.story: Alfirk's spectrum shows strong lines of helium, which only a very hot gas can excite, and that is the reading astronomers trust at the hot end, where the eye can say hot but no longer how hot. Most of the star's energy leaves as ultraviolet, so what reaches your eye is a small, blue-tilted fraction of its true output.

HR7121.question: What temperature gives Nunki its blue-white tint in the Teapot's handle?
HR7121.why: The Teapot's handle holds the hot end of the scale in Sagittarius.
HR7121.look: Nunki is the upper star of the Teapot's handle, blue-white in binoculars. Compare it with creamier Albaldah, about 6° to the north-east, and with orange Kaus Media on the spout side.
HR7121.answer: Nunki's surface is about 18,900 K, more than three times the Sun's temperature, so its light leans to blue. Albaldah, creamy white just to the north-east, is nearly three times cooler.
HR7121.story: In 2022 two of the great mirrors of the H.E.S.S. observatory in Namibia, built to catch faint flashes from gamma rays striking the air, spent moonlit nights unfit for that work measuring the width of Nunki's tiny disk. A disk's width together with all the light the star sends, ultraviolet included, fixes how much each square meter gives out, and so the temperature, without trusting the color. Hot stars are small and their disks minute, so each such measurement anchors the top of the scale.

HR6879.question: Why does the Teapot's base look white below orange Kaus Media?
HR6879.why: The bottom of the Teapot sits just below its orange spout star and much higher on the scale.
HR6879.look: Kaus Australis marks the bottom of the Teapot, about 5° below Kaus Media. It is a crisp white point beside that orange one; put both in the field and defocus slightly.
HR6879.answer: Its surface is about 9,500 K, more than twice Kaus Media's, so its glow tilts toward blue while its neighbor's tilts toward red.
HR6879.story: Kaus Australis sits close to the temperature at which hydrogen's dark lines are strongest. Hydrogen absorbs those colors only when its electron has been lifted one step up from the bottom, which a gas this hot does often. Cooler gas lifts too few electrons and hotter gas tears them away, so the strength of the lines rises and falls along the scale like a second thermometer.

HR6165.question: How can Antares' sibling be eight times hotter than Antares?
HR6165.why: Antares has a sibling two degrees away, born in the same family yet sitting at the opposite end of the thermometer.
HR6165.look: Put Antares at one edge of a wide field and sweep about two degrees south-east, toward the tail of Scorpius. Swing back and forth, deep orange against crisp blue-white, and defocus both slightly to judge the colors as small disks.
HR6165.answer: τ's surface is about 31,500 K, against about 3,700 K for Antares, a factor of more than eight from the same birth cloud. Antares was born heavier, aged faster and cooled as it swelled, while τ is still a hot young star.
HR6165.story: τ Scorpii is one of the standard stars astronomers use to define the hot end of the spectral sequence: other stars are classified by matching their lines to its lines. Its spectrum is rich in helium and has almost none of the metal lines that fill Antares' light, so one binocular sweep spans the two extremes the sky's thermometer is built on.

HR6527.question: How hot is the blue-white stinger of the Scorpion?
HR6527.why: The Scorpion's stinger, at the tip of the curling tail, is the hot end of the scale in Scorpius.
HR6527.look: Follow the tail of Scorpius to its hook: the bright stinger is Shaula, with fainter Lesath just beside it, both blue-white. Compare them with yellow-white Sargas, six degrees away at the bottom of the curl.
HR6527.answer: Shaula's surface is about 19,000 K, three times Sargas' temperature, which is why the stinger looks steely where the curl looks creamy. Shaula is really at least three stars, but its brightest hot member sets the color.
HR6527.story: Shaula's temperature is read from the strengths of its helium lines, which grow steadily as a gas heats past the white range and so keep working as a thermometer where color has stopped changing. By that reading its brightest member is several times hotter than the Sun, a figure the eye could never extract from its blue-white tint.

HR15.question: How hot is Alpheratz, the blue-white corner of the Great Square?
HR15.why: Along the northern side of the Great Square the colors run from ruddy Scheat to a crisp blue-white corner.
HR15.look: Alpheratz is the north-east corner of the Great Square, a crisp blue-white point in binoculars. Scheat, at the north-west corner, gives a fine orange contrast.
HR15.answer: Alpheratz's surface is about 12,900 K, three and a half times Scheat's temperature, so along one side of the Square you cross from orange-red to blue-white.
HR15.story: Astronomers read the temperature of stars like Alpheratz from a sharp step in their ultraviolet light, where hydrogen begins to absorb strongly. The size of that step changes steadily with heat, so it works as a thermometer far beyond the point where color stops helping, and for Alpheratz it confirms a surface a good deal hotter than any white star.

HR8781.question: How much hotter is Markab than Scheat, the corner directly north?
HR8781.why: The Square's south-west corner sits directly below ruddy Scheat on the sky and far above it on the thermometer.
HR8781.look: Markab is the Great Square's south-west corner. Compare it with Scheat directly north: crisp white against orange-red.
HR8781.answer: Markab's surface is about 10,500 K, at the high end of the published values, and Scheat's about 3,700 K, well under half that. Markab is also the nearer star, so distance and dust play no part in the contrast.
HR8781.story: Markab's disk is too small for any single telescope to show, but the CHARA Array on Mount Wilson has measured it, combining six telescopes to see detail like one instrument some three hundred meters across. Add up all the light the star sends, ultraviolet included, and that width says how much each square meter must give out, which pins the temperature without any help from the color. The result lands squarely among the white stars, a check on the thermometer by a route that never looks at color.

STAR-Algol.question: What temperature does Algol's blue-white stand for, eclipses aside?
STAR-Algol.why: The famous winking star of Perseus is also the hot end of its scale, its dimmings caused by a cooler companion.
STAR-Algol.look: Algol sits in Perseus, about halfway between Cassiopeia's W and the Pleiades. At full light it matches golden Almach, about 12° to the west, in brightness, which makes the two a fine color comparison: gold against blue-white.
STAR-Algol.answer: Its bright star's surface is about 12,550 K, roughly three times Almach's, and that sets the blue-white. The partner that eclipses it every 2.87 days is a cool orange subgiant, a second temperature hidden in the same point.
STAR-Algol.story: Algol's eclipses double as a thermometer. When the dim companion covers part of the hot star, the light falls by more than half, but when the hot star covers the companion half a cycle later, the dip is tiny. Each dip measures how brightly the hidden surface was shining per square meter, so the ratio of the two dips says how much hotter one star is than the other.

HR264.question: How hot is the blue-white star at the center of Cassiopeia's W?
HR264.why: The middle star of Cassiopeia's W is the hottest of the five, with orange Schedar right beside it.
HR264.look: γ Cas is the middle star of the W, a clean blue-white point in binoculars. Swing to orange Schedar, the next bright star west, and back.
HR264.answer: γ Cassiopeiae's surface is about 28,000 K, roughly six times Schedar's temperature, yet the difference in tint is only blue-white against orange. The disk of gas it sheds changes its brightness over the decades, while the star beneath stays much the same.
HR264.story: γ Cassiopeiae is a reminder that brightness can change while color stays put. Over the past century it has brightened and faded by more than a magnitude as its disk of gas grew and dissolved. Yet observers have always seen the same blue-white, and the temperature of the star beneath, read from its helium lines, has hardly moved.

HR472.question: What temperature lies behind Achernar's icy blue-white?
HR472.why: At the end of the long river of Eridanus a lone brilliant star closes the scale.
HR472.look: Look for the lone brilliant blue-white star at the end of the long, faint river of Eridanus. Binoculars show a sharp point; compare its icy color with creamy Alpha Hydri about 5° away.
HR472.answer: Achernar's surface is about 14,800 K, roughly two and a half times the Sun's temperature, so its glow tips firmly toward blue, the hot end of the scale in this part of the sky.
HR472.story: Achernar spins so fast that it is flattened, and a flattened star is hotter at its poles than at its stretched-out waist, by many thousands of degrees in its case. The blue-white you see is an average over that patchwork, weighted by how the star happens to be tilted toward us.

HR8425.question: What temperature makes Alnair shine such a clean blue-white?
HR8425.why: The Crane's brightest star sits a few degrees from orange-red Tiaki and at the opposite end of the scale.
HR8425.look: Center Alnair, then Tiaki, about 6° away in Grus: one is blue-white, the other orange-red. Defocusing both slightly makes the colors richer.
HR8425.answer: Alnair's surface is about 13,200 K, more than twice the Sun's temperature, which tilts its glow toward blue. Tiaki still gives out more light, being a giant, a reminder that color reads heat, not power.
HR8425.story: Alnair's spectrum shows the first faint lines of helium, which no cooler star can produce, because helium holds its electrons so tightly that only a very hot gas can make it absorb light. Those lines place Alnair firmly above the white stars, a reading that agrees with the bluish tint you see.

HR4730.question: How hot is Acrux, the blue-white foot of the Southern Cross?
HR4730.why: The foot of the Southern Cross is the hot end of a figure whose top star glows orange.
HR4730.look: Acrux is the bright star at the bottom of the Cross, blue-white in binoculars with a much fainter star beside it. Swing about 6° up to orange Gacrux at the top and back.
HR4730.answer: Acrux's surface is about 21,000 K, nearly six times Gacrux's temperature, so the Cross runs from orange-red at the top to blue-white at the foot. Both bright stars hidden inside Acrux are hot, so their blend keeps the same steely tint.
HR4730.story: Photographs of the Southern Cross show Gacrux as a gold jewel among blue ones, and camera sensors respond to color much as the eye does, so the contrast is no illusion of human vision. Measured through filters, Acrux is brighter in blue light than in yellow while Gacrux is far brighter in yellow, and that change of sign spans the scale from cool to hot within one small figure.

HR4853.question: Why do Mimosa and the Jewel Box's brightest stars share one icy color?
HR4853.why: On the eastern arm of the Cross, with the Jewel Box a degree away, a blue-white star shares its color with a whole cluster.
HR4853.look: Mimosa is the bright blue-white star on the eastern arm of the Cross. Put it at the edge of your view and look about 1° south-east for the Jewel Box, whose brightest stars share its icy color.
HR4853.answer: Mimosa's surface is about 27,000 K, and the Jewel Box's brightest members are hot young stars of the same kind, so the same heat paints them the same icy tint, near and far alike.
HR4853.story: Mimosa and the brightest stars of the cluster beside it are hot for the same reason: they are heavy, and a heavy star burns its fuel so fiercely that its surface runs tens of thousands of degrees. Such stars cannot last long, so a family full of them, and of their icy color, must be young.

HR5267.question: Why does Hadar look blue-white beside yellowish Alpha Centauri?
HR5267.why: The two Pointers make a calibration pair, and Hadar, beside Sun-like Alpha Centauri, sits at the hot end.
HR5267.look: Swing between the two Pointers, about 4° apart: Hadar is blue-white, Alpha Centauri warmer and yellower. In binoculars Hadar stays a single point, its three stars far too close to split.
HR5267.answer: Hadar's surface is about 25,000 K, more than four times Alpha Centauri's Sun-like 5,800 K, and the two Pointers show that gap as plainly as any two stars in the sky.
HR5267.story: Hadar's spectrum is rich in lines of helium, an element that only a very hot gas can make absorb light, while Alpha Centauri's is crowded with the metal lines of a Sun-like star. The two Pointers differ in their fingerprints as plainly as in their tints, and at Hadar's end of the scale it is the helium lines, not the color, that supply the number.

HR7790.question: How hot is the Peacock, the lone blue-white star of Pavo?
HR7790.why: In a sparse part of the far southern sky, the lone bright star of Pavo gives the scale its hot end.
HR7790.look: The Peacock is the bright blue-white star of Pavo, alone in a sparse field. Defocus slightly and its bluish tint holds steady against the few faint field stars around it.
HR7790.answer: The Peacock's surface is about 17,600 K, three times the Sun's temperature, so its glow tilts firmly toward blue. A hidden companion orbits it, but the hot primary sets the color.
HR7790.story: Beyond white, the eye's thermometer flattens: a star this hot peaks in the ultraviolet, and the visible tail of its glow slopes gently toward blue whatever the exact temperature. The Peacock's cold tint says hot, but only its spectrum can say how hot, and it is the spectrum, not the eye, that supplies the number on this card.

HR6510.question: How hot is the blue-white star of the Altar?
HR6510.why: Six degrees north of orange β Arae, the Altar's blue-white star closes the scale.
HR6510.look: Find α Ara below the tail of Scorpius, about six degrees north of orange β Arae. Side by side they make a fine contrast, blue-white against orange.
HR6510.answer: α Arae's surface runs at about 21,800 K, more than five times β Arae's temperature and nearly four times the Sun's. The disk of gas around its equator makes its brightness drift, but the heat of the star itself sets the color.
HR6510.story: α Arae's spinning disk of gas adds light of its own, mostly the red glow of hydrogen, so in principle it warms the star's color a touch. In practice the star beneath is so much brighter that the blend still reads blue-white, and its helium lines, untouched by the disk, give the temperature.

HR4199.question: How hot is the brightest star of the Southern Pleiades?
HR4199.why: The Southern Pleiades are led by a hot blue-white star at the top of the scale in Carina.
HR4199.look: Theta Carinae is the brightest of a loose group of blue-white stars visible even to the naked eye. In binoculars the group spans about a degree, a compact spray in the middle of the field, all sharing its bluish tint.
HR4199.answer: Its surface runs at about 31,000 K, more than five times the Sun's temperature. Even so its color is the same blue-white as stars a third as hot, because the eye cannot read heat this extreme.
HR4199.story: A star this hot pours most of its light out as ultraviolet, and its spectrum shows lines of helium strong enough to place it among the hottest stars of Carina. The eye, which sees only the visible tail of that glow, calls it simply blue-white, so the full measure of its heat comes from the spectrum and from satellites above the air.

HR3165.question: Why doesn't Naos, at the top of the scale, look deep blue?
HR3165.why: Naos sits at the very top of the scale in Puppis, one of the hottest stars the naked eye can see, and it tests how far the eye's thermometer can reach.
HR3165.look: In binoculars Naos is a sharp, steely blue-white point among many fainter Milky Way stars. Swing about 10° west to deep yellow-orange Pi Puppis and you have both ends of the scale in neighboring fields.
HR3165.answer: Its surface is about 40,000 K, nearly seven times the Sun's, so almost all of its output comes out as ultraviolet and the visible part we catch is only a gently sloping tail. That tail looks blue-white for any star hot enough, which is why the eye's thermometer tops out here.
HR3165.story: Heat this extreme turns light into a push. Naos's ultraviolet glare is caught by atoms in its own outer layers and shoves them outward, driving a wind that streams off at more than two thousand kilometers a second. That wind carries off mass many millions of times faster than the Sun's gentle breeze and will strip away a sizable part of the star, so here a temperature also foretells a star giving itself back to space.

DS-Albireo.question: Can you read two temperatures at once in Albireo's gold and blue?
DS-Albireo.why: Albireo puts two marks of the thermometer into a single binocular view, a final test of everything your eyes have learned tonight.
DS-Albireo.look: Albireo marks the head of the swan, at the foot of the Northern Cross. Brace your binoculars and at 10× it splits into a golden-orange star with a blue-white spark beside it, 34″ away; if the split is hard, let the image drift and watch the blue point trail behind.
DS-Albireo.answer: Your eye has just done what the spectra do, ranking the two by heat at a glance, and the gold one is cooler by some 8,600 degrees. Seen together under the same sky and through the same air, the difference can only be temperature.
DS-Albireo.story: Spectra read each of Albireo's stars separately and confirm what the eye sees: lines of metals and the first faint molecular bands in the gold giant's light, hydrogen and helium in the blue star's. That blue star spins so fast it has flung a disk of gas around its waist. Two temperatures leave two different kinds of fingerprint, and the eye catches the same difference as gold against blue.

DS-ThetaTau.question: Why does one star of the θ Tauri pair look white and the other yellow-orange?
DS-ThetaTau.why: θ Tauri is a naked-eye pair that holds two temperatures in one glance, and its stars are siblings, which makes the comparison especially fair.
DS-ThetaTau.look: Inside the Hyades V, about 2° from Aldebaran, look for an obvious wide pair that binoculars split at a glance. θ² is white and θ¹ yellow-orange, and a slight defocus makes the contrast stronger.
DS-ThetaTau.answer: θ² has a surface near 7,600 K, hotter than the Sun, while θ¹'s yellow-orange marks a surface cooler than the Sun's, so one small pair straddles our own star's place on the scale.
DS-ThetaTau.story: Two stars in one binocular field are the fairest color test there is, because their light passes through the same air at the same height, so the atmosphere reddens both equally. The eye also sharpens a contrast when two tints sit side by side, a trick of perception that makes θ¹ look a little more golden beside its white sibling than it would alone.

HR5763.question: How can two matched stars in Boötes show such different colors?
HR5763.why: The ν Boötis pair sets two colors side by side in one field, and because the two look equally bright, color is the only thing left to compare.
HR5763.look: Start at Nekkar, the star at the top of the kite of Boötes, and sweep east. Binoculars show orange ν¹ and white ν² side by side, nearly equal in brightness.
HR5763.answer: ν¹ is an orange giant with a surface near 3,900 K, while ν² is a white star thousands of degrees hotter, so the pair spans much of the scale in a single field. The eye ranks them in a moment, the warm one cool and the pale one hot.
HR5763.story: Each of the ν Boötis stars has had its temperature read from its spectrum, independently of its color, and both readings agree with what your eye reports: a cool giant beside a much hotter star. The orange one is also the larger and the farther of the two, a giant whose light travels more than twice as far to arrive looking just as bright as its neighbor.

HR7735.question: What temperatures hide in the orange and white stars of 31 Cygni?
HR7735.why: 31 Cygni sets two colors side by side with gaps wide enough for any binoculars, an easier cousin of Albireo's famous contrast.
HR7735.look: Binoculars show orange 31 Cygni with white 30 Cygni about 5½′ away and a fainter star closer in. The gaps are wide, so the colors come easily even at 7×.
HR7735.answer: The orange supergiant's surface is near 4,000 K, while white 30 Cygni beside it is a far hotter star, so one easy field shows two clear marks on the scale, with no bracing and no patience needed.
HR7735.story: Side by side, a warm tint and a cool one push each other apart, so the orange looks more orange and the white a little bluer than either would on its own. Astronomers avoid that bias with filters, but for a binocular observer it is a gift, because it makes the difference in temperature leap out of the field.

HR6262.question: Which star of the ζ Scorpii pair is the hot one?
HR6262.why: The ζ Scorpii pair puts two tints into one view, and the fainter, paler star turns out to be a test of the thermometer itself.
HR6262.look: Where the tail of Scorpius bends south, two stars sit a few arcminutes apart, an easy naked-eye pair: orange ζ² and fainter, paler ζ¹. From mid-northern sites the scene hugs the horizon and needs a clear southern view.
HR6262.answer: Pale ζ¹ is the hot one, a hypergiant near 17,000 K, but its light crosses so much dust that it arrives yellowed, the tint of a star near 6,500 K; orange ζ² is a nearby giant. Here the eye's thermometer is fooled, and only a spectrum shows the heat.
HR6262.story: A star's color can be tilted by what lies between it and you, because dust scatters blue light more than red, so astronomers never trust a color alone across a long, dusty path. They compare it with the temperature the spectrum gives from its pattern of lines, and the gap between the two, called the color excess, measures how much dust the light has crossed. Toward the tail of Scorpius, deep in the Milky Way, that gap can be large.

HR7139.question: Can you read two temperatures at once in the δ Lyrae pair?
HR7139.why: δ Lyrae holds an orange-red giant and a blue-white star in one field, two ends of the thermometer side by side.
HR7139.look: About 3½° north of Sheliak, in Lyra, δ² Lyrae glows orange-red, with fainter blue-white δ¹ about a third of a Moon-width to the west. Defocus slightly and the colors deepen.
HR7139.answer: δ² runs a touch cooler than Betelgeuse, while blue-white δ¹ belongs with Vega at the hot end, so one field holds nearly the whole scale. Your eye reads it in under a second; it took spectra to put numbers on it.
HR7139.story: Swap your eye for a camera with a blue filter and the pair trades places: δ¹, the fainter star to the eye, becomes the brighter of the two, because so little of cool δ²'s glow falls at the blue end. Through a yellow filter δ² is about three times the brighter; through a blue one δ¹ is about one and a half times the brighter. That swing between filters is the color index astronomers turn into a temperature.
